**The example is deliberately unfinished.** Of the ten components in `parking/`, three run: the
contract, the web app, and the database. The other seven have a README stating their contract and no
code. That is not a gap in the material; it is the material. The documents were written before the
code on purpose — Part I's argument that nothing in software has mass — and a difference between
what the documents say and what the code does is work to be done, not an error in the documents.

**Where to start.** If you have an hour: the taxonomy of unknowing in Part I, "Nobody hands you the
problem" in Part II, and the pivot in Part III. If you have an afternoon, read it in order; each
part assumes the one before it and says so where it leans on it.

**Conventions.** Requirement IDs like `S-8` refer to `parking/REQUIREMENTS.md`, where every "must"
has a test that names it. `K0`–`K4` are defined at the start of Part I and again, briefly, at the
start of Parts II and III. A file name in `code` links to the chapter that renders it, or to the
file in the repository.

## Part I — The discipline

*Why we work this way: what engineers are for, and what most of the practice is actually managing.*

## 1. Why We Work This Way

What this course thinks the discipline is, and why the rest of the repository is shaped the way it
is.

| Document                  | Answers                            |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `SOFTWARE-ENGINEERING.md` | why we work this way               |
| `AGENTS.md`               | how agents work here               |
| `CONTRIBUTING.md`         | how a change is accepted           |
| `parking/REQUIREMENTS.md` | what the system must observably do |
| `parking/DESIGN.md`       | how we intend to achieve it        |

Nothing in this file is checkable by continuous integration. That is exactly why it has to be
written down: the parts of engineering that no tool enforces are the parts that get lost, and then
rediscovered at full price.

---

### 1.1 What engineers are for

**Engineers make reliable things, on time, within resource constraints, in a way that manages
discomfort for the team, the client, and the users.**

Four constraints that trade against each other, and a fifth — scope — that is usually the honest one
to move. A plan that does not say which of them is fixed is not a plan; it is a wish with dates
attached.

Note that *reliable* is not *correct*. Correctness is a property of a program measured against a
specification. Reliability is a property of a system running in a world that contains bad inputs,
hostile inputs, failing hardware, wrong clocks, partial networks, and people. The gap between those
two words is where most of the work is, and `parking/` is built almost entirely inside it.

#### Discomfort is a first-class variable

| Whose      | What it looks like                             | What reduces it                          |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| The users  | confusion, wasted time, distrust of the answer | the product actually being good          |
| The client | surprise                                       | frequent, honest, boring status          |
| The team   | fear, thrash, heroics, weekends                | slack, small steps, reversible decisions |

This is not about comfort as a goal. Fear degrades judgment, and a frightened team abandons exactly
the practices that would have prevented the fear. Discomfort is a leading indicator — usually the
earliest one available, arriving weeks before the schedule shows anything.

---

### 1.2 Why software engineering differs

Software engineering has two advantages the older disciplines do not, and between them they account
for most of what follows:

- **Tests are cheap.** You cannot build a second bridge to find out whether the first one holds. You
  can run a suite a thousand times before lunch. What follows from that is "The cost of testing
  changes everything".
- **Software has no gravity.** Nothing sags or cracks to tell you it is wrong, so every signal a
  physical structure gives away for free has to be built here on purpose. What follows from that is
  "Nothing has mass".

The two pull in opposite directions, which is why neither is simply good news. Cheap tests make
certainty affordable; the absence of gravity is what makes it necessary to go buy some, because a
bad design will hold itself up indefinitely, at full speed, with the tests passing.

---

### 1.3 Most of practice is being less nervous

Backups. Version control. Tests. Code review. Short iterations. Client demos. Staging environments.
Each is normally taught as a rule to follow. Each is better understood as a way of retiring one
specific fear, and you should be able to name which.

| Practice               | The fear it retires                         |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Backups                | "I could lose the work."                    |
| Version control        | "I can't get back to when it worked."       |
| Tests                  | "I don't know if I just broke something."   |
| Continuous integration | "It works on my machine."                   |
| Short iterations       | "We are building the wrong thing."          |
| Client demos           | "They will hate it in month six."           |
| Code review            | "Only one person understands this."         |
| Signed commits         | "Nobody vouched for this code."             |
| Fault injection        | "I don't know what happens when it breaks." |

Two consequences follow, and both are load-bearing:

- **A practice that reduces no one's anxiety will be abandoned under pressure.** Ceremony that costs
  time and returns no relief gets dropped in week ten, and it should be. If you cannot name the fear
  a practice retires, either find it or stop doing it.
- **A practice that reduces anxiety without reducing risk is worse than nothing.** A backup nobody
  has restored. A test suite that cannot fail. A green dashboard measuring the wrong thing. These
  are the most dangerous artifacts in engineering, because they spend the alarm and leave the danger
  in place.

---

### 1.4 The taxonomy of unknowing

| #      | Category            | What it is                                                           |
| ------ | ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **K0** | The known           | Things you know, that are true.                                      |
| **K1** | The known unknown   | Things you know you don't know.                                      |
| **K2** | The unknown unknown | Things you didn't know you didn't know.                              |
| **K3** | Erroneous certainty | What feels like K0 and is false.                                     |
| **K4** | True falsehoods     | Things we hold as true, knowing they aren't, because they're useful. |

**K0 through K3 are in order of expense.** Looking something up is cheap. Researching a question you
have already framed is more. Being surprised costs a rewrite. Being confidently wrong costs whatever
was built on top of the belief, discovered at the worst possible moment. K4 is not on that ladder at
all — it is a choice, and a good one.

**Building something is the act of discovering, in the right order and at the right price, which
category each part of a problem domain belongs to.** Every practice in this repository is a way of
moving something down the ladder before it charges full price.

| From | To     | How                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ---- | ------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| K0   | stays  | Write it down so it stays known: tests are executable knowledge, and unlike prose they complain when they go stale.                                                                           |
| K1   | K0     | Spikes, prototypes, reading the source, asking the client. Cheap, and available on demand — the only category you can simply decide to spend money on.                                        |
| K2   | K1     | Exposure to reality, early and repeatedly: integrate, deploy, demo, inject faults, watch real use. You cannot search for these; you can only arrange to be surprised sooner and more cheaply. |
| K3   | K0     | Evidence: a test that could have failed, an output you actually looked at, a signature you checked, a second person who does not share your assumption.                                       |
| K4   | chosen | Name the falsehood, write down where it is load-bearing, know the blast radius when it comes due.                                                                                             |

*Figure (on the web page): K0 through K3 in order of expense. Looking something up is cheap; being confidently wrong costs whatever was built on the belief. Every practice in the repository moves something down the ladder before it charges full price. K4 is not on the ladder: it is a falsehood chosen, recorded, and kept.*

#### K3 is the one to be afraid of

K1 and K2 are honest. K3 is expensive precisely because it costs you nothing at the time — no search
is triggered, no question is asked, no ticket is filed. You are not looking, because as far as you
know there is nothing to look for.

Only two things find K3: reality, and someone who does not share your assumption. That is the entire
justification for running the code instead of reasoning about it, for integrating early, for review
by a person rather than by yourself an hour later, and for `F-6`, which requires every attack to be
*demonstrated before its defense is built*. "I verified the signature" is K3 until you have
personally forged a reading and watched the check reject it.

#### K4: the falsehoods we keep on purpose

Every abstraction is a chosen falsehood. `parking/` holds a stack of them, and each is written down
somewhere in `REQUIREMENTS.md` precisely because it is false:

- The clock is correct. (`N-2`, `N-5`, and the `skewed` fault say otherwise.)
- The network delivers. (`C-1` exists because it doesn't.)
- The sensor is honest. (`F` is a catalogue of ways it isn't.)
- Capacity is constant. (`S-6`: a mismatch is a fault, not a correction.)
- The token reflects the user's current role. (It reflects their role up to eight hours ago.)

The engineering act is not avoiding these — you cannot build anything without them. It is choosing
them deliberately, recording them, and knowing what breaks when one comes due. An abstraction leaks
exactly where its falsehood was load-bearing. **A K4 you have chosen is an asset; the same falsehood
held unknowingly is K3.**

---

### 1.5 Time

Tie a string to a rat that has learned one side of the cage is electrified, and measure how hard it
pulls away as it is drawn toward that side. The pull is not linear. It is nearly flat far out and
rises steeply as the distance closes — an *avoidance gradient*, roughly `1/x` in shape.

Deadlines do this to people. The month before ship feels like nothing; the last week is unbearable.
The exact curve is a metaphor, not a measurement, but the shape is the part that matters, and it has
a vicious property: **the spike arrives exactly when the project can least afford the behavior it
produces.** Skipped tests, bundled diffs, unreviewed merges, "we'll clean it up after launch." The
fear near the deadline destroys the practices that would have made the deadline survivable. That
feedback loop, not incompetence, is how most projects actually fail.

The engineering response is not willpower. It is to change the terrain.

- **Remove the danger.** If deploying is routine and reversible, the shore stops being electrified.
  An always-releasable trunk means shipping is not an event.
- **Build the bridge.** A thin end-to-end slice — click to route to SQL to response — built early
  and then thickened, crosses the gap. Horizontal layers all finish at the same time: never.
- **Put small fences along the way.** Intermediate checkpoints flatten the curve, but only if they
  are real. A demo to an actual client, a conformance run that exits nonzero, a deploy that
  happened. A status meeting is not a fence; it discharges no fear, because nothing was proved.
- **Keep slack.** A plan at full utilization has no capacity to absorb K2, and K2 is guaranteed.
  Queues do not degrade gracefully near full utilization; latency goes to infinity. Slack is not
  waste, it is the budget line for the unknown unknown.
- **Estimate the category, not the task.** "Two days" usually means "two days if nothing I haven't
  thought of happens" — a K0 statement about a schedule governed by K2. Work sitting in K0 estimates
  well. K1 work estimates as a range. K2 work cannot be estimated at all, only time-boxed. Say which
  kind you are handing over.
- **Bad news early is a gift; bad news late is a betrayal.** A two-week slip found in week two is a
  planning problem. The same slip found in week eleven is a crisis. The delay in reporting, not the
  slip, is what makes it expensive — and hiding it is the most common way engineers create the
  client discomfort they were trying to avoid.

---

*Figure (on the web page): The avoidance gradient: nearly flat far from the deadline and steep at the end — arriving exactly when the project can least afford the behavior it produces. Fences that prove something flatten the curve. A status meeting does not, because it discharges nothing.*

### 1.6 The cost of testing changes everything

**The first structural difference between software engineering and the other engineering disciplines
is the cost of a test.** You cannot build a second bridge to see whether the first one stands. A
wind tunnel hour is expensive, a mask set is expensive, a recall is catastrophic. So those
disciplines front-load everything — analysis, simulation, review, sign-off — before anything is cut.
Waterfall is not a bad habit inherited from the 1970s; it is the correct response to a test that
costs a million dollars and takes a year.

Software's tests can be free, run in a second, and run ten thousand times a day. Nearly everything
filed under "agile" is downstream of that single fact. Three things follow that are usually left
out:

**1. It is per decision, not per project.** Both regimes live inside this one repository. Changing a
route handler is seconds to verify. Changing a schema under a database with real data in it is not
(`V-7`). A released firmware image cannot be recalled (`G`). A private key that has leaked cannot be
unleaked (`I-2`, `I-7`). A published interface with users on it is a promise (`V-4`). So you run
waterfall locally, around the expensive-to-test decisions — think it through, review it, get it
right the first time — and agile around the cheap ones. Methodology is a function of the cost of
being wrong once, and that cost can change twice in an afternoon.

**2. The cost of a test is designed, not given.** Lowering it is ordinary engineering work with a
known toolkit: pure functions, deterministic seeds (`T-1`), faults driven through a control plane
instead of waited for (`F-1`, `T-2`), one command back to a known state (`T-5`), conformance
checkable from outside (`T-4`), and logs that record the inputs that drove a decision so a failure
explains itself (`C-9`). **Lowering the cost of a test is often the highest-leverage work available,
because it multiplies against every future change.** And the inverse is diagnostic: *if something is
hard to test, that is information about the design, not about testing.*

**3. Testing is one feedback loop among several.** Each has a cost, a latency, and a fidelity, and
they catch different classes of error:

| Loop                 | Latency | Catches                                                     |
| -------------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| Running the thing    | seconds | "it doesn't work at all"                                    |
| Unit test            | seconds | broken logic, regressions                                   |
| Integration test     | minutes | wrong assumptions between components                        |
| Human review         | hours   | unclear intent, missing cases, bad design                   |
| Client demo          | days    | building the wrong product                                  |
| Production telemetry | live    | everything you didn't imagine — at the worst possible price |

Push each class of error down to the cheapest, fastest loop that can catch it. But notice that some
errors are only catchable by an expensive loop: no test suite in the world detects "we built the
wrong thing." Only a person looking at it does.

Two properties of a loop matter more than its coverage:

- **A test that cannot fail proves nothing.** Watch it fail first — which is why `CONTRIBUTING.md`
  requires that the test fail without the change. A test written after the fact, never observed red,
  is a K3 generator with a green checkmark.
- **A loop you do not trust is worse than none.** Flaky tests train a team to ignore red, and after
  that the suite that would have caught the real one has been disarmed. `T-1` bans unseeded
  randomness for this reason, not for tidiness.

---

### 1.7 Nothing has mass

The second difference is physical, and it shows up first in the schedule.

Drywall goes up after plumbing. Not by convention — the pipe occupies the space the wall will cover,
and matter cannot be threaded through matter after the fact. The frame follows the foundation
because it rests on it. Every arrow in a Gantt chart in the older disciplines is, at bottom, a fact
about mass: one thing must physically exist before the next can be attached to it, and the
half-finished intermediate states are real objects that cost real money.

Software is massless. A function can be called before it is written. Nothing occupies the space
another thing will need. There is no partially-poured anything.

So when a software schedule says *"we can't start B until A is done,"* that arrow is almost never a
fact about the world. It is a fact about the design: **B does not know what A will look like.** The
dependency is an unwritten interface, and it is being paid for in calendar time.

**The design goal is a flat chart** — everything startable at once. The mechanism is one the
discipline already owns, used deliberately instead of incidentally:

| The dependency says          | The artifact that dissolves it                    |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| "B needs A's shape"          | an interface — signature, schema, error codes     |
| "B needs A to answer"        | a mock that answers, and misbehaves on request    |
| "B isn't done until A works" | a test that fails today and passes when A arrives |

None of the three requires A to exist. The dependency does not get sequenced, it gets **specified**
— which is why `contract/` is layer 0 and was built first while seven of the components that will
use it are still only READMEs. The promise is what unblocks, not the implementation. `collector/`
gets a folder while running in-process for the same reason: *so that the interface is real before
the network is.*

**The cost is real and has to be paid on purpose.** A mock is a K4 — *the real component will behave
like this* — false the day you write it. Flattening the chart does not delete the dependency; it
converts a **scheduling** risk into an **integration** risk. That is a good trade only if you
integrate continuously. Mock everything, integrate at the end, and you have built the worst artifact
in this document: every team delivered on time and the system does not work. That is the Time
section's horizontal-layers failure arriving through a side door.

Two rules keep the trade good:

- **The mock and the real thing must be interchangeable under the same tests.** That is what `T-4`
  is for — conformance checkable from outside means the fake and the shipped sensor answer to one
  specification, so swapping them is an event with a result rather than a discovery.
- **Sequence around irreversibility, not around incompleteness.** The orderings that genuinely
  survive in software are the one-way doors — a schema with data under it (`V-7`), a distributed key
  (`I-2`), a released image (`G-3`) — plus the honest case where you must learn something before you
  can design against it, and a spike is the mock for that. Every other arrow in the chart is a
  confession that an interface has not been written down.

One warning follows from the same property. Mass supplies error signals for free: a bad structure
sags, cracks, or falls down, and nobody has to be clever to notice. **Software has no gravity, so
nothing collapses to tell you.** A bad design holds itself up indefinitely, at full speed, with the
tests passing. Every feedback loop in the previous section exists to replace the signal that mass
would have given away.

---

### 1.8 Failure is an input, not an exception

Most specifications describe the happy path and inherit the rest by accident — whatever the HTTP
library happens to do on timeout becomes the product's behavior, chosen by nobody.

For every input a component depends on, four cases need a stated answer: **absent, late, wrong, and
lying.** `parking/` exists to force those four questions on every consumer, which is why the sensor
is a designated liar with a switchboard.

A system that only works when its inputs behave is not finished. And an adversary is just the
unknown that optimizes: **security is this same discipline applied to an input chosen specifically
to find your K3.**

---

### 1.9 Interfaces, reversibility, and the installed base

- **Spend deliberation in proportion to reversibility, not to how interesting the decision is.**
  Renaming a variable is free to undo. A data format with data already in it, a published URL, a
  distributed key, an artifact someone installed — those are one-way doors. Most arguments in
  software are conducted at the wrong intensity for their reversibility.
- **The moment a second party depends on your interface, it stops being a decision and becomes a
  promise.** `V-4` is that idea made precise, and versioning (`V-1`–`V-5`) is the mechanism for
  keeping the promise while still being allowed to change.
- The property being engineered is the **cost of the next change**. Anyone can write the first
  version. The design shows its worth in the second, which is also when nobody remembers why the
  first was shaped that way — so write that down while you still know.

---

### 1.10 Provenance

Every claim in a system has an author, and the question that runs through this entire repository is:
**who said this, and can I check it later without asking them again?**

It is the same question at every layer — a reading (`S-8`, `I-5`), a log record (`L-9`), a firmware
image (`G-2`), a commit (`CONTRIBUTING.md`). The device registry and `.github/allowed_signers` are
the same structure one layer apart, and noticing that is the point.

Provenance is the mechanical answer to K3. "I'm sure this is right" is a feeling. "This is signed by
a key in the registry, and here is the check" is evidence. And on the human side, a signature is a
person saying *I have read this and I stand behind it* — which cannot be delegated, and which the
arrival of capable agents makes more important rather than less.

---

### 1.11 Scale, recovery, availability

Three questions the system answers at runtime whether or not anyone wrote them down. Unstated, the
answer is whatever the implementation happened to do — chosen by nobody, and discovered in
production.

| Requirement      | The question that forces it                                         | An answer looks like                  |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| **Scale**        | How many actual users? And lots, readings a second, rows in a year? | an order of magnitude, plus a horizon |
| **Recovery**     | What happens when X breaks — and what does it take to get back?     | a procedure someone has run and timed |
| **Availability** | How much downtime is tolerable, for whom, per what period?          | a number with a period                |

**Scale.** "A city" is not a number. Eight lots, one sensor each, a reading every thirty seconds,
twenty thousand drivers on a Friday evening, ninety days of history — those are design inputs; the
first is a mood. Precision is not the point; the order of magnitude is, and so is everyone holding
the same one. Postgres and a five-second poll is the obviously right answer at ten lots and an
obviously wrong one at a million sensors, and nothing about the code says which world it is in. Ask
for the number *and its horizon* — "and in two years?" — then write down the number you are
explicitly **not** designing for, which is the cheapest scope decision available and ends the same
argument permanently. The number is K4: false the day you write it. Written down it is an asset with
a known blast radius; assumed, it is the K3 that rewrites get named after.

**Recovery.** "What happens when X breaks" is two questions, and the second is the one that gets
skipped. First: what does the system do *while* X is down — degrade, wait, refuse, serve stale, and
does the user learn which? That is what `C` and `U-1` are for. Second: what does it take to get back
— who does it, with which command, from which backup, and how long does it take? That answer is real
only if someone has run it and timed it; a restore procedure nobody has executed is the canonical
anxiety-reducing artifact with the risk left in place. Answer both per component, not for "the
system": the answer for a sensor (poll it again in five seconds) is nothing like the answer for the
database (restore, and lose everything since the last backup — how much is that, in minutes?). That
last figure is itself a requirement, not a consequence: **how much data may we lose** has to be
decided by someone entitled to decide it.

**Availability.** Downtime tolerance is a budget with a period and a beneficiary: the driver-facing
page may be down four hours a month; the ops UI may be down a day; a single missed poll bothers
nobody. Different components deserve different budgets — that is exactly what lets you spend the
money where it matters. Two things make this worth forcing early:

- **The unstated default is 100%**, which is the most expensive requirement you can accidentally
  accept, and it quietly forbids deploys, restarts, and schema migrations (`V-7`). A team that never
  gave itself a maintenance budget cannot do the "remove the danger" move from the Time section,
  because every release is an incident.
- **The number chooses the architecture** — mostly by choosing whether a human is allowed in the
  loop at all:

| Budget | Down per month | What it implies                                         |
| ------ | -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| 99%    | 7 hours        | a person can notice and fix it                          |
| 99.9%  | 43 minutes     | alerting that pages, and a runbook someone has run      |
| 99.99% | 4 minutes      | no human in the loop: redundancy and automatic failover |

None of these three is ours to choose alone — they are client answers, and on day one each costs one
sentence. Later they cost a migration, a rewrite, or an outage, in that order.

---

### 1.12 Security, ethics, and law are requirements

Three more permanent members of the requirement set, and the easiest of all to postpone: no user
files a ticket for them, they compete against visible features, and their absence looks exactly like
their presence right up until it doesn't.

Two properties make deferring them a mistake rather than a trade-off:

- **Their deadline is set by someone else** — a breach, an audit, a complaint, a regulator, a
  journalist. You do not get to schedule it into the next sprint.
- **Violations are the irreversible kind.** Data that leaked cannot be unleaked. A person harmed is
  not fixed by a patch. These are one-way doors, and the earlier section applies at full force.

In practice:

- **Security.** Write down the threat model: who the adversary is, what they can do, what they want.
  Then design against that, not against a vague sense of danger. Every dependency is a transfer of
  trust and a permanent obligation; know where you have placed it and why.
- **Law.** Mostly about data — what you collect, how long you keep it, who you must notify, what you
  may reuse. Also licensing and the provenance of code, which now includes code an agent produced.
  Note that `A-5` puts retention deliberately outside the reach of any API: that is a legal design
  as much as a security one.
- **Ethics.** The people affected who are not in the room — non-users, bystanders, the surveilled.
  Parking data is location data about people. *"Counts, not locations"* in `REQUIREMENTS.md` is an
  ethical decision wearing technical clothes: it is nearly free to make now and nearly impossible to
  retrofit later. Data minimization is the cheapest protection that exists — the safest record is
  the one you never kept. Accessibility and translation live here too (eight language packs are not
  decoration), as does the question of what the system does to the person whose lot shows the wrong
  number.

**The cheapest moment to satisfy all three is while the requirements are still soft.** After that
you are not adding a requirement, you are performing a migration.

---

### 1.13 People are part of the system

- **Coordination cost grows faster than the team.** Adding people to a late project makes it later.
  The fix is smaller, clearer interfaces between people — not more meetings.
- **The system will resemble the communication structure that built it.** If that is going to happen
  anyway, choose the structure on purpose.
- **The deliverable is not the code.** It is the code plus the ability of someone else to run it,
  reset it, deploy it, diagnose it at 3am, and continue it in month seven. "It works on my machine"
  is a claim about a machine.
- **Maintenance is most of the total cost**, and the reader you are writing for is most often
  yourself, having forgotten. This is why `AGENTS.md` treats attention as the scarce resource.
- **Write down what you decided not to do.** The `Scope decisions` and `Non-goals` sections of
  `REQUIREMENTS.md` are the cheapest documentation in this repository: they end the same argument
  three times and tell the future why the obvious thing was not done.
- **Distribute discomfort deliberately and visibly** — on-call, review load, the tedious work.
  Burnout is a systems failure with a schedule, not a personal failing, and it shows up as
  attrition, which is the uncontrolled deletion of K0 with no backup.

---

### 1.14 Working with agents

An agent is an extremely fast writer with no stake in the outcome. It moves the economics of this
discipline in exactly one direction: **the cost of producing code has fallen much faster than the
cost of knowing that the code is right.** Everything scarce therefore migrates to the second half —
specification, verification, review, ownership.

In the taxonomy, an agent is a K3 factory. Fluent, confident, plausible, and occasionally wrong is
the precise shape of erroneous certainty, now arriving faster than you can check it. That is not an
argument against using agents. It is an argument about where to spend the time they save.

- **Spend the speed on lowering the cost of testing** — fixtures, harnesses, seed data, fault
  scripts, conformance checks, the boring second test case. That work multiplies. More features do
  not.
- **Review capacity is now the bottleneck.** Ask for diffs you can actually read, one concern at a
  time.
- **Never let confidence substitute for a run.** "This should work" is K3 by construction.
- **Delegation is not abdication.** You sign it, so you own it — and if you cannot explain it, you
  cannot maintain it or defend it. Working code you cannot explain is a liability in this
  repository, not an asset.

#### Nothing important may live only in a head

A design constraint that exists only in a developer's head has always been a liability. It used to
be a survivable one: the person holding it sat nearby, saw the change, and said "no, not like that"
in the hallway. With agents in the loop that recovery path is gone. An agent is not in the hallway,
does not know the constraint exists, and will hand you a clean, tested, plausible violation of it
faster than you can read the diff.

So the state of the project has to be **observable from where every party stands** — the client, the
humans, and each agent, which arrives knowing nothing and leaves remembering nothing. An unwritten
constraint fails in both directions at once: the holder's belief that everyone knows it is K3, and
for everyone else it is K2 — you cannot ask about something you have no idea exists.

#### The working set

What "observable" requires will keep changing as the tools do. Today it means four documents, in the
repository, versioned alongside the code — not in a wiki, not in chat history, not in a notebook:

| Document          | Answers                                                                                        | Written by        |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------- |
| `REQUIREMENTS_vX` | what must observably be true                                                                   | us and the client |
| `DESIGN_vX`       | how we intend to achieve it, and what we rejected                                              | us                |
| `QUEUE`           | what is being worked, in what order, by whom, and what would make it done                      | us                |
| `FINDINGS`        | what we learned the expensive way — surprises, dead ends, measurements, the attack that worked | reality           |

- **`_vX`, because a superseded requirement is not deleted knowledge.** Editing in place destroys
  the before-picture, and the diff between two versions is the most useful conversation the client
  ever has with you. Same idea as `V-4` one layer up: once a second party depends on a statement,
  changing it is a version, not an edit.
- **`QUEUE` is the shared cursor.** Without one, two workers do the same task twice, or each assumes
  the other has it. That failure was always possible with people; it is now cheap to hit ten times
  in an hour.
- **`FINDINGS` is the K2/K3 ledger,** and the only one of the four that reality writes. A fact
  discovered at full price and not written down gets rediscovered at full price. An agent has no
  memory of last week's dead end — and increasingly, neither do you.

These are not project-management ceremony. Each retires a specific fear — "we are building different
things," "nobody knows what state this is in," "we already learned this once" — and by the earlier
rule, a document that retires no fear should be dropped rather than maintained.

#### Context is a budget, and it resets every session

An agent starts from nothing, every time. On a real system it cannot read the project to find out
what is going on: it does not fit, and even where it fits, reading everything in order to change one
thing is the wrong price. So *how does a competent stranger find the five files that matter, in ten
minutes, without reading the other five hundred?* stops being a nicety and becomes a load-bearing
property of the repository.

The good news is that this is the same property that makes a codebase habitable for people. Clear
component boundaries, a README per component stating its contract, stable IDs like `S-8` that grep
from a test back to the sentence that demanded it, a dependency rule that can be checked
mechanically, names that mean what they say — humans navigate by these, and so do agents.
**Factoring done for human comprehension pays twice.**

The bad news is that several conventions that genuinely helped human readers now cost real money:

| Convention                            | What it costs now                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A doc-comment on every function       | Spends context restating what the signature already says — and prose goes stale silently, where stale prose reads exactly like true prose. K3, pre-delivered. |
| One enormous file                     | Cannot be read in part, so every task pays for all of it.                                                                                                     |
| Deep indirection in the name of reuse | The seam-hiding tax, charged to humans and agents alike.                                                                                                      |
| Commented-out code, historical asides | Ambiguous authority: is this the specification, or the past?                                                                                                  |

The replacement is not "no documentation." It is self-documenting code, a hint exactly where the
code cannot say *why*, and everything durable in the working set, where both kinds of reader look.
That is the rule `AGENTS.md` already gives for comments; agents did not change it, they only put a
price tag on breaking it.

#### Ask your agents

Models are changing faster than this document can. Any specific advice about how to prompt, how much
to hand over at once, or what an agent can be trusted to do unsupervised has a short shelf life —
the conventions just above included.

The durable move is to ask the model you are actually using: *what did you have to read that you
should not have needed? what would have let you get this right the first time? what did you assume
because nobody wrote it down?* Then put the answer in the repository rather than the chat, where the
next session — human or not — will find it. Treat it as a proposal from something with no stake in
the outcome, like any other advice here. But ask, because the alternative is a convention tuned for
a model that has already been retired.

---

### 1.15 Where this shows up in `parking/`

| Idea                          | Where it is made concrete                                          |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Reliability vs. correctness   | `C`, `F`, `U` — everything about inputs that misbehave             |
| K3 → evidence                 | `F-6`: demonstrate the attack before building the defense          |
| K4, named and recorded        | `N` (clocks), `S-6` (capacity), the `skewed` fault                 |
| Provenance                    | `S-8`, `I-5`, `L-9`, and signed commits in `CONTRIBUTING.md`       |
| Cost of testing, designed     | `T-1`, `T-2`, `T-4`, `T-5`, `F-1`                                  |
| One-way doors                 | `V-7` (migrations), `G-3` (rollback), `I-2` (keys)                 |
| Flat chart, by contract       | `contract/` at layer 0, and seven components specified but unbuilt |
| Ethics in the requirements    | "Counts, not locations"; `A-5`; the language packs                 |
| Fences, not heroics           | `npm run check`, `parkctl conform`, one-command reset              |
| Scale, recovery, availability | `E` — 100 lots, five seconds a day, one hour at 2am                |

---

### 1.16 If you want the longer arguments

- Fred Brooks, *The Mythical Man-Month* — coordination cost, and why adding people makes it later.
- Fred Brooks, "No Silver Bullet" — essential versus accidental complexity.
- Richard Cook, "How Complex Systems Fail" — eighteen paragraphs, and the best return per page here.
- Michael Nygard, *Release It!* — failure as an input, with the patterns named.
- Nancy Leveson, *Engineering a Safer World* — safety as a system property, not a component
  property.
- Forsgren, Humble, and Kim, *Accelerate* — the measured case that fast feedback and reliability are
  the same variable, not a trade.

## 2. Agile and Waterfall

The shape of software engineering: two orders for the same six steps, the one fact that decides
between them, the words people use, and the failure that looks exactly like progress.

| Document                  | Answers                                                                    |
| ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `SOFTWARE-ENGINEERING.md` | why the cost of a test is the first structural difference                  |
| `AGILE_VS_WATERFALL.md`   | what shape that difference gives the work, and the vocabulary              |
| `TESTING.md`              | what "(test)" means at each step                                           |
| `docs/TEAM-AND-CLIENT.md` | the iteration, the demo, and the client                                    |
| `parking/REQUIREMENTS.md` | a requirements document that stayed at the top of the waterfall on purpose |

`SOFTWARE-ENGINEERING.md` says that waterfall is the correct response to a test that costs a million
dollars, and that nearly everything filed under "agile" is downstream of software's tests being
cheap. It mentions waterfall and does not describe it. This document does, because the shape
matters: students do not fail by choosing the wrong methodology. They fail by sliding down the steps
of the one they did not choose, faster than they notice.

### 2.1 Terms used here

| Term             | Meaning                                                                                                                                                 |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **K0–K4**        | The five kinds of not-knowing, from `SOFTWARE-ENGINEERING.md`. K2 is the unknown unknown; K3 is confident and wrong; K4 is a falsehood kept on purpose. |
| **Fence**        | A checkpoint that proves something: a demo, a deploy, a test that could have failed. A meeting is not one.                                              |
| **One-way door** | A decision that cannot be cheaply undone: a schema with data under it, a published interface, a distributed key, a released image.                      |
| **Observable**   | Checkable from outside without reading the source. Requirements are written in it.                                                                      |

---

### 2.2 The same six steps

Both shapes are made of the same six steps, and the steps are in the right order in both. You cannot
design against a requirement you do not have; you cannot build a design you have not chosen; you
cannot deploy what you have not built.

| Step         | What it produces                                                                             | The question it answers        |
| ------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Requirements | numbered, observable statements of what must be true — and what is *not* being built         | what, for whom, and how much   |
| Design       | chosen mechanism: the tables, the protocols, the keys, the components, and what was rejected | how, and why not the other way |
| Develop      | code that a second person can read and defend                                                | does it exist                  |
| Test         | evidence that the code does what the requirement says                                        | does it work                   |
| Deploy       | the thing running where its users are, and a way back                                        | is it out there, and healthy   |
| Maintain     | everything after: fixes, changes, upgrades, the next request                                 | is it still true               |

The disagreement between the two shapes is not about the order. It is about the **batch size** and
about **where the tests are**.

---

### 2.3 Waterfall, described

Waterfall runs the six steps once, in order, each finished and signed off before the next begins:

```
Requirements → Design → Develop → Test → Deploy → Maintain
```

Winston Royce drew it in 1970 and, two pages later, wrote that the implementation as drawn "is risky
and invites failure," because testing arrives at the end, where every surprise costs the most. The
industry kept the drawing and dropped the warning.

It is worth being fair to the shape, because outside software it is correct. A civil engineer cannot
build a second bridge to see whether the first one stands. A chip designer pays for a mask set once.
When the only real test costs a million dollars and a year, the rational response is to move
everything that can be checked *before* that test: analysis, simulation, review, sign-off, change
control, a requirements document that is frozen because changing it means re-doing the analysis.
Waterfall is what a discipline looks like when it cannot afford to be wrong twice.

| What waterfall retires                                       | What it creates                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| "we will spend the money on a design that was never checked" | "we will find out it was the wrong product at the end, at full price" |
| "the requirements moved under us"                            | "the requirements were frozen before anyone had seen the thing"       |
| "nobody signed off"                                          | "everyone signed off, and it was still wrong"                         |

The right-hand column is what happens when the shape is applied to work whose tests are cheap. K2 —
the surprise you could not have asked about — is guaranteed on every project, and waterfall
schedules its arrival for the last step.

---

### 2.4 Agile, described

Agile runs the same steps in loops, with a test inside every step rather than a Test step at the
end. Three loops, three latencies, three different instruments:

```
Release loop       (weeks; reality answers)
  Iteration loop   (days; a person answers; time-boxed, and scope is what moves)
    Requirements   (test: the client reads a precise claim and objects; K4s read back)
    Design         (test: a contract, a mock that misbehaves, a spike, a failing test)
    Develop        (test: red, then green — the seconds loop)
    Demo           (test: a person drives the real thing)              ← the fence
  Deploy           (test: health-gated, automatic revert, rollback timed)
  Observe          (production telemetry; what K2 arrived → FINDINGS)
  Delete           (what can we remove?)
There is no Maintain step. After the first deploy, every iteration is maintenance.
```

Five things about the shape are load-bearing:

- **"(test)" means something different at each step.** Requirements are tested by a person — the
  client reading a sentence precise enough to be wrong. Design is tested by artifacts that exist
  before the code: a contract two people can build against, a mock that misbehaves on request, a
  spike, a test that fails today. Develop is tested by red then green. Deploy is tested by a health
  check with a timeout and an automatic revert. Leave the label off and students will hear "unit
  test" four times. `TESTING.md` spells each one out.
- **The iteration ends on a fence, not on "done."** A fixed period — one to two weeks — that ends
  with a running thing in front of a human. When the period ends, scope is what moves. Without the
  time box the inner loop is not a loop, it is a spiral.
- **The demo is the only instrument for "wrong product."** No test suite detects that you built
  exactly what was asked and nobody uses it. A person driving the real thing does, and that is why
  the demo closes the inner loop rather than decorating it.
- **The outer loop's product is knowledge.** Deploy answers "does it survive reality"; Observe
  writes down what reality said (`FINDINGS`); Delete returns the carry nobody schedules. The
  distinctive output of agile is not more code sooner. It is K2 converted to K1 at the cheapest
  available price, in the right order.
- **Maintain is not a step because it is the loop.** Waterfall drew maintenance last and smallest
  and put most of the money there. Agile has no line between building and maintaining: the second
  iteration after the first deploy is the same shape as the first.

---

### 2.5 The distinction is the cost of a test

Everything in section 2.3 is legal for one reason: a test can be free, run in a second, and run ten
thousand times a day. That is what lets Requirements be wrong on Monday and corrected on Tuesday,
lets a design be a contract and a mock instead of a signed-off drawing, and lets Deploy be routine
instead of an event.

So the choice between the shapes is not a preference. It is **determined, per decision, by the cost
of being wrong once** — and both regimes live inside one repository:

| Decision                                       | Cost of being wrong once                              | Regime                                              |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| a route handler, a translation string, a query | seconds to find out, seconds to undo                  | loop: change it, run it, keep or revert             |
| the derived `available` column                 | every consumer, but all inside one repository         | loop, with the tests that name `S-1` and `U-1`      |
| a schema with real data under it (`V-7`)       | a migration inside a one-hour window (`E-8`)          | **waterfall, locally**: think, review, migrate once |
| a published API with clients on it (`V-4`)     | a version served alongside the old one, forever       | waterfall: it is a promise now, not a decision      |
| a distributed private key (`I-2`)              | cannot be unleaked                                    | waterfall, and a ceremony                           |
| what data about people you collect             | cannot be un-collected; a regulator sets the deadline | **waterfall, before anything else**                 |

Read the right-hand column top to bottom and notice that the regime changes as the door becomes
harder to reverse. Around a one-way door you run a small waterfall *inside* the loop: get the
requirement exactly, design it on paper, review it with someone who does not share your assumption,
and do it once. Everywhere else you loop. Methodology is a function of the cost of being wrong once,
and that cost can change twice in an afternoon.

The last row is the subject of the next section, because it is the door students walk through
without noticing there was a door.

---

### 2.6 Falling down the waterfall

Here is the failure, and it looks like a productive week.

A team is asked for a campus parking app. By Tuesday there is a schema: `students(id, name, plate)`,
`vehicles(plate, student_id)`, `sightings(plate, lot, seen_at)`, third normal form, an index on
`(lot, seen_at)`, a view that joins all three, a query that answers "where did this student park
last Thursday" in eleven milliseconds. It is good work. Everyone is comfortable.

In week four the client is asked — late, in passing, per the intake question about who is affected
who is not in the room — whether student identity may be joined to a location. The registrar's
answer is no: not without consent, and consent is not on the table. Whether the rule is the federal
privacy law for student records, the institution's own policy, or a data-protection law that applies
because one user is abroad does not matter to the schema. What matters is that `sightings` cannot
exist in the form it has, the join is forbidden, the view is forbidden, the query is forbidden, and
the user interface built on the view has no data. The whole plan was misguided by a rule that lives
at the top of the waterfall, and the team spent four weeks at the bottom.

`parking/` carries the one-line requirement that would have saved the month: **"Counts, not
locations."** It is in `Scope decisions`, it has an ethical reason attached in
`SOFTWARE-ENGINEERING.md`, and no amount of database normalization would ever have produced it. It
comes from a question, not from a design.

#### Why the slope is there

Software has no mass, so this is not gravity. It is the **comfort gradient**. Each step down the
waterfall is more concrete, more familiar, more solitary, and produces something you can see: a
table, a query, a screen. Each step up is more ambiguous, more social, and produces a document
nobody grades. Reading a privacy law is uncomfortable. Asking a registrar a question is
uncomfortable. Writing a sentence precise enough for a client to reject is uncomfortable.
Normalizing a schema is a pleasure.

`SOFTWARE-ENGINEERING.md` makes discomfort a first-class variable and says that people abandon the
practices that would have saved them at exactly the moment the fear peaks. This is the same
mechanism earlier in the project: people go where *their own* discomfort is lowest, which is the
bottom of the waterfall, and leave the client's and the users' discomfort — surprise, and a product
that cannot legally exist — for later. The slope of the waterfall is the developer's comfort
gradient, drawn as a diagram.

Agents make it steeper. An agent will produce the normalized schema, the indexes, and fifty queries
in a minute, and it will never ask about the registrar unless a requirement says to. It falls down
the waterfall at machine speed.

#### The tells

You are falling when any of these is true before there is a numbered requirement the client has
objected to:

- There is a schema.
- There is a framework, a language, or a library chosen.
- There is a "temporary" table, column, or default.
- "We'll figure out login later." "We'll add the privacy stuff at the end."
- There is no `Non-goals` list, so nothing has been refused yet.
- Nobody can say who, outside the room, this system keeps a record about.

#### The railing

The engineering response is the one the essay gives for fear: do not rely on willpower, change the
terrain. Put fences at the top of the waterfall so that descending early is visibly a violation
rather than an instinct.

1. **Ask the expensive questions first.** The questions whose answer could *invalidate* the plan
   come before the questions whose answer only *shapes* it. What data about people does this keep?
   Who is entitled to see it? What law or policy applies, and who says so? How many, and in two
   years? How long may it be down? What are we not building? Each is a sentence to ask and a month
   to discover. `docs/TEAM-AND-CLIENT.md` has the full list; this is the subset with a regulator
   attached.
2. **Write the answer where it cannot be missed.** `Scope decisions`, `Non-goals`, and a section of
   the requirements for security, law, and ethics — three permanent members of the requirement set,
   as the essay says, with deadlines set by someone else.
3. **Read the K4s back.** "We're assuming a record of where a person parked is fine to keep. True?"
   converts the whole example above into one sentence in week one.
4. **Only then descend — and descend on purpose.** A *spike* is a permitted descent: time-boxed,
   aimed at one question, its code thrown away. Falling is a descent with no question and no time
   box. The difference is whether you can say, before you start, what you will know when you stop.

`parking/` was built this way on purpose, and its history shows it: after the original demo arrived,
the first commits were the requirements, the design, the policy, and a contract — documents and a
layer-0 folder, before a single feature. The seven components that are still only READMEs are not
behind schedule. They are waiting at the top of the waterfall until their requirement is settled.

---

### 2.7 Requirement, or design?

Students have trouble telling these apart, and the confusion is expensive in a specific way: a
requirement cannot change without the client, and a design can. Put a design decision in the
requirements and you have promised the client a table name. Put a requirement in the design and it
can be quietly changed by whoever edits the file next.

Two questions separate them, and a sentence must pass both to be a requirement:

> **Could a different team satisfy this sentence a different way?** **Could you check it from
> outside, without reading the source?**

| Requirement (what must be observably true)                               | Design (the mechanism we chose)                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A stale count is never presented as current (`U-2`)                      | The collector stamps receipt time; staleness is computed from `age_ms`                  |
| Every reading is attributable to a device (`S-8`)                        | Ed25519 over an ordered, pipe-joined signing string                                     |
| One command returns the system to a known state (`T-5`)                  | `docker compose down -v`                                                                |
| Revocation takes effect no later than the next poll (`I-4`)              | The collector reads the `devices` table every cycle, so there is no cache to invalidate |
| Student identity is never joined to a location                           | `sightings` has no `student_id` column, and no view that could add one                  |
| A lot under maintenance reads as closed for service, not missing (`E-9`) | A `maintenance` state distinct from `down` in the derived-state enum                    |

The tells that a requirement has design in it: a table name, a library, a language, an HTTP status
code, an endpoint path, an algorithm. The tells that a design has a requirement in it: "the user
must be able to," with no mechanism following. And the rule from `CONTRIBUTING.md`: a pull request
that edits a requirement to match what the code happens to do is a design change wearing a costume.

Keeping them apart is what makes the loop cheap. The design can be replaced in an iteration; the
requirement is renegotiated with a person. `DESIGN.md` says it in its first paragraph: every
mechanism there is replaceable without renegotiating a requirement.

---

### 2.8 From a user story to an API

The other thing students find hard is the middle: they can write a story and they can write an
endpoint, and they cannot see how one turns into the other. The chain has four links, and the third
is the one that gets skipped.

```
user story → acceptance criteria → acceptance test → observables the test needs → the contract
 who, what,    observable,            fails today       fields, states,               the API
 and why       numbered                                 endpoints
```

**A story** names a person, a want, and a reason: *As a driver arriving for an event, I want to see
which lots have space, so that I can go straight to one instead of circling.* The reason is the part
that matters; it is the pain, and the want is a guess about the solution.

**Acceptance criteria** turn it into observable sentences, each of which can be wrong: the page
shows a count per lot; a count older than the staleness threshold is shown with its age and never as
current; a lot whose data cannot be trusted reads as unknown, not missing. Those are `U-1`, `U-2`,
and `U-3` — a story became three numbered requirements.

**The acceptance test** is one of those sentences made executable, and it is written to fail today.
In the style of `T-2`, driven through the sensor's control plane:

```
set lot 3's sensor to `stuck`          # 200 OK, frozen as_of
poll past the staleness threshold
GET the driver view
assert lot 3 shows a count with an age, and is not marked current
```

**The observables** are what the test had to reach for in order to assert anything. To assert "with
an age," the driver view must expose an age. To assert "not marked current," it must expose a state.
To drive the fault, the sensor must have a control plane. So the test *forces* fields into
existence: `age_ms`, a derived `live`/`stale`/`unreachable`, `POST /control/mode`. Those fields are
the contract — `S-1`, `C-4`, and the control table in `REQUIREMENTS.md` — and they exist because a
test needed to observe them, not because someone thought they would be nice.

That is the whole trick. **An API is the set of observables your acceptance tests need.** Design the
tests and the API falls out; design the API first and you will ship fields nobody can test and miss
the ones somebody needed.

The VIP story from `docs/TEAM-AND-CLIENT.md` runs the same chain and shows it producing something
harder. *As a season-ticket holder, I want to hold a space for thirty minutes, so that I am not
circling when I arrive.* Criteria: a hold is visible to its holder with its expiry; the last space
goes to exactly one of two simultaneous requests; a retried request does not take a second space.
Tests: two concurrent holds, assert one wins; the same request twice, assert one hold. Observables
forced: an `expires_at`, an idempotency key on the request, and a race decided in one database
statement. The test for "exactly one wins" is what puts the decision inside the database rather than
in whichever request the load balancer saw first — the design was chosen by the test.

Two consequences:

- **A story with no test is a wish.** It cannot be wrong, so it cannot be finished.
- **A test with no story is accidental complexity.** It protects something nobody asked for, and it
  will be maintained forever.

`T-3` is this chain as a rule: every "must" has a test that names its ID. Grep the ID and you walk
from the test back to the sentence, and from the sentence back to the person.

#### The scoreboard

The chain has a side effect that is worth more than it looks. When tests are named by the story or
requirement they serve, and grouped that way in the output, a test run stops being a count of passes
and becomes a board: *these stories are green, those are still red, this one turned green today.*
That is gamification — progress shown as a score people want to move — in the only form that is
honest, because every point on the board could have been lost. A team watches its own board turn
green in groups that mean *a driver can now do this*. A client reads the same board without reading
a line of code, and it is a fence they can check between demos. `T-3` gives `parking/` the board for
free: run `node --test` and the names carry the IDs, so sorting the output by `U-`, `C-`, `S-` is
sorting it by promise.

The board is only honest while the tests are. The moment a green can be produced without the
behavior — a test that asserts nothing, a skipped suite that reports success — the score detaches
from the thing it measured, and the game is being played against yourself.

---

### 2.9 The words people use

Each term with what it is, what it is *for* — the fear it retires, since a practice that retires
none will be dropped in week ten — and what this repository calls it.

| Term                                 | What it is                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | The fear it retires                                          | Here                                                     |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Iteration / sprint**               | A fixed period, one to two weeks, ending at a fence. Scrum's word is *sprint*.                                                                                                                                                                                            | "we are building the wrong thing, and won't know for months" | the iteration in `docs/TEAM-AND-CLIENT.md`               |
| **Time box**                         | The period is fixed; scope moves. The opposite of "until it's done."                                                                                                                                                                                                      | "it will never end"                                          | the fence ends it                                        |
| **User story**                       | A person, a want, a reason, on a card. A pain plus a guess.                                                                                                                                                                                                               | "we lost the *why*"                                          | section 2.7                                              |
| **Acceptance criteria**              | The observable sentences a story must satisfy, numbered.                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | "we each heard something different"                          | the `U`, `C`, `E` requirements                           |
| **Acceptance test**                  | A criterion made executable, written to fail first.                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | "we think it's done"                                         | `T-2`, `T-3`                                             |
| **Definition of done**               | The checklist a change must fully pass. Not most of it.                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | "done means different things to different people"            | `CONTRIBUTING.md`                                        |
| **Backlog**                          | Everything not yet done, in priority order, each item with a done sentence. The product backlog is all of it; the sprint backlog is this iteration's slice.                                                                                                               | "nobody knows what's next"                                   | `QUEUE`, held by the Queue role                          |
| **Spike**                            | A time-boxed investigation to answer one question. The code is thrown away.                                                                                                                                                                                               | "we can't estimate this because we don't understand it"      | K1 to K0, on purpose (section 2.5)                       |
| **Stand-up / daily scrum**           | Five minutes, every day: done, next, blocked — and since when.                                                                                                                                                                                                            | "I didn't know you were stuck"                               | section 2.3 of the guidebook                             |
| **Sprint review / demo**             | The client drives the real thing at the end of the iteration.                                                                                                                                                                                                             | "they will hate it in month six"                             | the demo rules                                           |
| **Retrospective**                    | The team, alone, after the demo: what did we learn the expensive way?                                                                                                                                                                                                     | "we already learned this once"                               | `FINDINGS`                                               |
| **Scrum**                            | A named framework: three accountabilities (product owner, scrum master, developers), five events (the sprint, planning, daily scrum, review, retrospective), three artifacts (product backlog, sprint backlog, increment). Everything in this table with capital letters. | the fears above, packaged                                    | the four roles are the same shape, sized for four people |
| **Product owner**                    | The one voice who orders the backlog and can say yes, no, and how much.                                                                                                                                                                                                   | "the client is five people who disagree"                     | the Client role, and one voice on their side             |
| **Increment**                        | The running thing at the end of an iteration. Usable, or it doesn't count.                                                                                                                                                                                                | "we have lots of parts and no product"                       | the thin vertical slice                                  |
| **Minimum viable product**           | The smallest increment that answers the question "would anyone use this?"                                                                                                                                                                                                 | "we built the whole thing before asking"                     | iteration one of `parking/`                              |
| **Velocity**                         | Work completed per iteration, in whatever unit the team uses. A planning input, never a target — the moment it is graded, estimates inflate.                                                                                                                              | "we can't plan"                                              | not tracked here, deliberately                           |
| **Gamification**                     | Progress shown as a score people want to move: tests turning red to green, grouped by story. Honest only while every green could have been red.                                                                                                                           | "we can't see progress"                                      | tests named by requirement ID (`T-3`)                    |
| **Kanban / WIP limit**               | A board with a cap on how much is in progress at once. Finish before starting.                                                                                                                                                                                            | "everything is half done"                                    | the Queue role's cursor                                  |
| **Pair programming**                 | Two people, one keyboard. Review while writing; K0 in two heads.                                                                                                                                                                                                          | "only one person understands this"                           | pair on the scary parts                                  |
| **Refactoring**                      | Changing structure without changing behavior, under tests that prove it.                                                                                                                                                                                                  | "we can't touch this"                                        | serve, don't rule (`TESTING.md`)                         |
| **Technical debt**                   | Carry you took on knowingly, to be repaid. Unknowing carry is not debt; it is just cost.                                                                                                                                                                                  | "we don't know what we owe"                                  | `Deferred` in `DESIGN.md`                                |
| **Continuous integration**           | Every push is built and tested on a machine that is not yours.                                                                                                                                                                                                            | "it works on my machine"                                     | `CONTRIBUTING.md`'s three checks                         |
| **Continuous delivery / deployment** | Every green build *could* ship (delivery); every green build *does* ship (deployment).                                                                                                                                                                                    | "release is an event"                                        | `E-6` makes the second one a requirement                 |
| **Trunk-based development**          | Everyone commits to one always-releasable branch, in small steps; long-lived branches are the enemy.                                                                                                                                                                      | "the merge will take a week"                                 | `main`, signed                                           |
| **Feature flag**                     | A switch that lets code ship dark and turn on later. Decouples deploy from release.                                                                                                                                                                                       | "deploying it means users see it"                            | the sensor's `MODE` is one                               |

Two warnings about the vocabulary. First, none of it is the point; each term is a fear-retirement
with a name, and a team that performs the ceremonies without the fears will drop them under pressure
and be right to. Second, the terms are Goodhart bait — velocity most of all. When a measure becomes
a target it stops measuring.

---

### 2.10 What keeps humans and agents comfortable

The essay makes discomfort the leading indicator. The shape of the work is where you control it.

**Humans are comfortable when the next step is small, visible, and reversible.** Concretely:

- They know what *done* means before they start, because it is a sentence in the queue.
- They can see the fence — the demo is on the calendar, the deploy is routine — so the fear near a
  deadline has nothing to attach to.
- Decisions are two-way doors wherever possible, so being wrong costs an afternoon.
- There is slack in the plan, so K2 arriving is a planning event and not a crisis.
- They can watch tests turn from red to green in groups that mean a story is satisfied — the
  scoreboard in section 2.7. Progress that is visible, honest, and theirs is the cheapest comfort
  there is, and the client draws the same comfort from the same board.
- Bad news early is rewarded, visibly, every time, so it arrives early.
- Nobody is blamed for K2. The retro says *findable by X; X is now on the list*, and does not say
  who should have asked.
- The uncomfortable top-of-waterfall work is made concrete: a checklist of questions, a numbered
  document, a K4 to read aloud. Discomfort shrinks when the task has a shape.

**Agents do not feel anything, and the analogue is exact:** what keeps an agent *reliable* is the
same list, made literal, because an agent arrives every session knowing nothing and leaves
remembering nothing.

- It needs the working set in the repository — `REQUIREMENTS`, `DESIGN`, `QUEUE`, `FINDINGS` —
  because there is no hallway in which to be told the constraint.
- It needs a task small enough to review, with a test that defines done, because review capacity is
  the bottleneck and "this should work" is K3 by construction.
- It needs the contract before the code, because it will otherwise invent one, fluently, and every
  session will invent a different one.
- It needs the K4s written down, because a K4 held only in a head is a K2 to the agent and it will
  hand you a clean, tested violation.
- It needs one command to run and one to reset, because a machine that cannot run the thing cannot
  check its own claim.

And one asymmetry that decides where the human stands. The bottom three steps of the waterfall are
where an agent is fastest and most useful: designs, code, tests, fixtures, migrations, the second
and third test case. The top three are where it is no help at all, because they are conversations
with people, laws, and a client's sense of proportion. So the arrival of agents moves the human *up*
the waterfall. The requirement document is the railing that keeps a machine-speed descent from
becoming a machine-speed fall, and the "(test)" at each step is how the human stays in the loop
without reading every line.

---

### 2.11 Checklists

**Before leaving Requirements for Design**

- [ ] Every requirement is numbered and observable, and the client has objected to at least one.
- [ ] `Scope decisions` and `Non-goals` exist and have been read aloud.
- [ ] The questions with a regulator attached have named answers: what data about people, who may
      see it, what rule applies, and who said so.
- [ ] The K4s have been read back as questions.
- [ ] Every "must" has, or is assigned, a test ID.

**Before leaving Design for Develop**

- [ ] Every one-way door is named, and each got the small-waterfall treatment: reviewed by someone
