Working agreement for AI agents contributing to this repository. Repository mechanics (how to run
things, what the code does) live in `CLAUDE.md`.

### 7.1 Who owns this

**Humans own the structure. Agents author and advise.**

The humans here are computer science students, and their goal is fluency: being able to read,
explain, change, and defend every part of this system without help. An agent that produces working
code a student cannot explain has made the repository worse, not better. Correctness is necessary;
comprehension is the point.

The test for a change is not "does it work." It is "can a student read this next week and say why it
is here."

Everything an agent writes is a draft until a human accepts it. Make rejection cheap: small diffs,
one concern at a time, nothing bundled in that wasn't asked for.

### 7.2 Write for human attention

Attention is the scarce resource in this repo — not tokens, not runtime, not lines of code.

- **Smallest change that does the job.** Solve the problem in front of you. Related improvements you
  noticed are worth a sentence at the end, not a diff.
- **Boring over clever.** When two versions work, ship the one that needs less explanation.
- **No speculative structure.** No interface with one implementation, no config value that is never
  varied, no helper called once, no layer added for a requirement nobody has stated.
- **Dependencies cost attention.** Each one is something a student must learn, trust, and audit.
  Prefer what is already in `package.json` and the standard library. Adding a dependency is a
  proposal, not a decision.
- **Keep the seams visible.** A student should be able to follow a request from browser click to
  `fetch` to route to SQL to response by reading the code. Indirection that hides that path has to
  earn its place.

### 7.3 Comments

- Comment the *why*: a constraint, a trade-off, a gotcha, something that surprised you. The *what*
  is already in the code.
- Do not narrate obvious lines. A comment on every line trains students to stop reading comments.
- Match the comment density of the file you are editing.
- If code needs a paragraph to explain, first try to make the code need less explanation.
- Design rationale and alternatives considered belong in the conversation, not in the file.

### 7.4 Limit your own fluency

You write code more fluently than this repository needs. Spend that fluency on finding the simple
version, not on demonstrating range.

- Write the version a second-year student would write, and would recognize a month later.
- Three plain statements beat one dense chain.
- Do not reach for an exotic language feature because it is tighter.
- Do not optimize what is not slow. Note where it would matter, and move on.
- Do not rename, reformat, or reorganize code you were not asked to touch. Unrequested diff noise is
  the fastest way to lose a reader's trust.

### 7.5 Advising

- Give one recommendation and the reason it wins. If the call is genuinely close, say so in a
  sentence and still pick.
- State plainly what you are unsure about.
- Raise a real concern once, then do the work as asked. The human decides.
- When the task is something a student is meant to learn: do it if asked, then say what to read and
  what to try next.
- Never assert something about this code you have not opened the file to check.

### 7.6 Process

- Propose before restructuring. Moving directories, adding a build step, or introducing a service is
  a conversation first.
- Leave the repository runnable. If a change needs a manual step (a rebuild, a database reset), say
  so in the same breath.
- Say what you did not do, and why. Silent omissions are worse than open ones.

## 8. How a Change Is Accepted

How work gets from written to accepted in this repository.

`AGENTS.md` says humans own the structure and agents author and advise. This document is where that
stops being a statement and becomes a procedure.

### 8.1 Signing your work

**Every commit on `main` is signed.** Not as ceremony — it is the mechanical form of ownership. An
agent can write a diff; only a person can sign it, and signing is the act of saying *I have read
this and I stand behind it*.

Use SSH signing. You already have an SSH key for GitHub, and GPG key management is where this
practice usually dies in a classroom.

```sh
git config --local gpg.format ssh
git config --local user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
git config --local commit.gpgsign true
git config --local gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile .github/allowed_signers
```

Add yourself to `.github/allowed_signers`, one line per person:

```
you@example.edu namespaces="git" ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAA...
```

Check your own work before pushing:

```sh
git log --show-signature -1
```

That file is a **registry of humans**: a mapping from identity to public key, with enrollment and
revocation. It is the same structure as the device registry in `parking/DESIGN.md`, one layer up.
Recognizing the pattern in two places is the point.

### 8.2 Working with agents

Agents draft. People sign. Concretely:

- **Read the whole diff before you commit it.** If you cannot explain a line to someone else, it
  does not go in. Working code you cannot defend is a liability here, not an asset — the goal of
  this repository is fluency, and an unexplained dependency on a generated answer is the opposite.

- **Credit the agent, keep the authority.** Add a trailer; the signature stays yours.

  ```
  Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
  ```

- **Ask for smaller drafts.** An agent will happily produce three hundred lines. A diff you cannot
  review is a diff you cannot sign.
- **Push back in the conversation, not in the commit.** If the design is wrong, argue it before it
  becomes history.

### 8.3 Definition of done

A change is done when all of these are true. Not most.

- [ ] It satisfies a stated requirement, and the commit message names the ID (`C-4`, `L-9`, …).
- [ ] A test references that same ID and fails without the change.
- [ ] `docker compose up --build` works from a clean checkout.
- [ ] The full check suite passes locally.
- [ ] Anything now untrue in `REQUIREMENTS.md`, `DESIGN.md`, or `CLAUDE.md` is updated in the same
      commit. Documentation that drifts is worse than none, because people trust it.
- [ ] New behavior that can fail has a fault mode or an attack demonstration, per `F-5` and `F-6`.
- [ ] The commit is signed.

### 8.4 Requirements, design, and this file

Three documents, three questions, and changes belong in exactly one of them:

| Document                  | Answers                      | Changes when          |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------- |
| `parking/REQUIREMENTS.md` | what must be observably true | the goal changes      |
| `parking/DESIGN.md`       | how we intend to achieve it  | the mechanism changes |
| `CONTRIBUTING.md`         | how work is accepted         | the process changes   |

If a pull request edits a requirement to match what the code happens to do, that is a design change
wearing a costume. Say which one you mean.

### 8.5 Pull requests

**One concern per pull request.** Reviewer attention is the scarce resource in this repository, and
a bundled diff spends it on separating things that should never have been joined.

Include: what changed, which requirement IDs, how you verified it, and what you deliberately left
out. The last one matters most — silent omissions are the expensive kind.

Reviewers are asking three questions, in order:

1. Does it do what the requirement says, and does the test prove it?
2. Could a student read this in a month and explain why it is here?
3. What does it make harder later?

### 8.6 What continuous integration enforces

Anything that is merely a convention is not a policy. These run on every push:

```sh
# 1. every commit in the range is signed by a known key
git log --format='%H %G?' "$BASE..HEAD" |
  awk '$2 != "G" { print "unsigned or untrusted: " $1; bad = 1 } END { exit bad }'

# 2. conformance — the same CLI ops uses, exit code is the verdict
parkctl conform --all --json

# 3. integration — faults driven through the control plane, not waited for
docker compose -f docker-compose.test.yml up --abort-on-container-exit
```

The conformance checker is one program doing three jobs: the ops tool, the CI gate, and the grading
harness. That is why it takes `--json` and returns a meaningful exit code, and why it never prompts.

### 8.7 Local loop

```sh
cd parking
docker compose up --build      # full system
docker compose down -v         # reset; required after any schema change
parkctl conform --all          # what CI will run
```

`CLAUDE.md` covers what the code does and where things live. Read `AGENTS.md` before pointing an
agent at any of it.

---

## Part V — The essentials

*The tools, in the order a student needs them, each in the same shape: the fear it retires, the fence you prove, and what to do when it goes wrong.*

The tools, in the order a student needs them. Each document has the same shape — the fear it
retires, the fence you prove, a model, once per machine, once per repository, every day, when it
goes wrong, a checklist, and where it shows up in `parking/` — so that once you have read one you
can guess how the next is organized.

Read them in order. Each one assumes the one before it, and each ends with something you can
demonstrate.

| #   | Read                | The fear it retires                                                       | The fence you prove                                                                    |
| --- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 0   | `SHELL.md`          | "I don't know where I am, or what I'm typing into."                       | a fresh terminal lands in `~/projects` and you can read a `git clone` line             |
| 1   | `GIT.md`            | "I can't get back to when it worked." "Nobody vouched for this."          | `ssh -T` greets you; a commit shows **Verified** on GitHub                             |
| 2   | `1PASSWORD.md`      | "A secret is in the repo." "I'm locked out."                              | `parking/` runs with a secret injected by `op run`; recovery codes are in the vault    |
| 3   | `GITHUB-ISSUES.md`  | "Nobody knows what's being worked on, or why, or whether anyone read it." | an issue closed by a reviewed, green, merged pull request that names it                |
| 4   | `GITHUB-ACTIONS.md` | "It works on my machine." "Nobody ran the tests."                         | a green run on every push, running the command you run, with the badge                 |
| 5   | `DOCKER.md`         | "It works on my machine." "I can't get to a clean state."                 | `up --build` from a clean clone; `down -v` returns the seed; you know the architecture |
| 6   | `PACKAGES.md`       | "A different install broke it." "That CVE has been open a year."          | a committed lock, an install that refuses drift, one update merged green               |
| 7   | `AGENT.md`          | "Working code nobody can explain."                                        | an agent-drafted change you read, ran, signed, and can explain                         |

Two rules for the series, borrowed from the essays:

- **A tool that retires no fear is not essential**, and a document about it should be dropped. Each
  of these names its fear in the first table so you can hold it to that.
- **The fence is not optional.** A green run that could not have been red proves nothing; a setup
  you have not demonstrated is a setup you believe in. Do the fence, then read the next one.

`SHELL.md` is where to start if you have never opened a terminal. `GIT.md` is where to start if you
have.

## 9. The Shell

Everything else in this sequence is typed into a terminal. This is the one you read first so that
the rest of them make sense.

- **The fear it retires:** "I don't know where I am, or what I'm typing into."
- **The fence you prove:** From a fresh terminal: `cd ~/projects && pwd && which git && echo $HOME`
  prints what you expect, and you can explain every character of `git clone
  git@github.com:<user>/<repo>.git`.
- **Before this:** nothing
- **After this:** `GIT.md`

### 9.1 The model

A shell is a small program that reads a line, splits it into words, runs the first word as a
command, and hands it the rest as arguments. That is all. Every fancy thing it does is built on that
one sentence.

```
you ──type──▶ terminal ──line──▶ shell ──runs──▶ program
                                   │                │
                          environment: $HOME,      stdin  ◀── keyboard, or a pipe
                          $PATH, $PWD, ...         stdout ──▶ screen, or a pipe, or a file
                                                   stderr ──▶ screen (even when stdout is redirected)
                                                   exit code: 0 means ok, anything else means not
```

Four things a program gets from the shell, and the fourth is the one people forget:

- **A working directory.** `pwd` prints it. Every relative path is relative to it. Half of "no such
  file" is being in the wrong one.
- **An environment.** Named strings, inherited by every program you start. `$HOME` is your home
  directory. `$PATH` is the list of directories searched for a command; "command not found" means
  the program is not in one of them. `printenv` shows them all.
- **Three streams.** Input, output, and errors. `|` connects one program's output to the next's
  input. `>` sends output to a file; `>>` appends; `2>&1` folds errors into output so a pipe sees
  both.
- **An exit code.** Zero is success. `echo $?` shows the last one. Continuous integration, `npm run
  check`, and every script in this repository use it as the idiot light: the number is the verdict,
  and the text is just for humans.

### 9.2 Once per machine

**Windows.** Two options, and the second is the one this course assumes.

- *git-bash* from git-scm.com: a bash shell with git. `C:` appears as `/c/`.

- *Windows Subsystem for Linux.* Open PowerShell as administrator and run `wsl --install`, which
  gets you the current Ubuntu. Launch it, let it finish, create a user with no spaces in the name,
  then:

  ```sh
  sudo apt-get update
  sudo apt-get upgrade -y            # takes a while
  sudo apt-get install -y build-essential cmake git
  ```

  `C:/Users/<you>` is `/mnt/c/Users/<you>` inside WSL. It is tempting to keep projects there so
  Explorer can see them. Do not: files under `/mnt/c` cross a compatibility layer that is much
  slower for the many-small-files pattern git and compilers have, and a build that takes seconds in
  the Linux filesystem takes minutes there. Keep projects in your WSL home (`mkdir ~/projects`) and
  reach them from Explorer by typing `\\wsl$` in the address bar.

**Mac.** Terminal is built in. Install the command-line tools, which include git:

```sh
xcode-select --install
```

**Ubuntu.** The same three `apt-get` lines as WSL; you are already on Linux.

**Which shell.** Macs use `zsh`; Linux and WSL use `bash`. They agree on everything in this
document. `echo $SHELL` tells you which you have; the startup file is `~/.zshrc` or `~/.bashrc`, and
that is where a line like `export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"` goes if you need one.

**An editor that knows about the terminal.** Visual Studio Code has a terminal pane, a source
control pane, and a merge-conflict view that `GIT.md` relies on. On Windows install the *WSL*
extension so that VS Code runs against the Linux side; then `code .` from any WSL directory opens
that directory. On Mac, run *Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH* once from the command
palette.

**A place for projects.** One directory, in your home, with a short lowercase name: `~/projects`.
Not `Projects` — why hit shift a thousand times — and not `p` either; the shell has tab completion.
On campus Windows machines your home may be a network drive with too little space and too much
latency for build artifacts; use `C:/Users/<you>/projects` there, and let git be the backup.

### 9.3 Every day

| Want                     | Type                                           | Note                                                      |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| where am I               | `pwd`                                          |                                                           |
| what is here             | `ls -la`                                       | `-a` shows dotfiles like `.git` and `.env`                |
| go somewhere             | `cd ~/projects/parking`                        | `cd` alone goes home; `cd -` goes back                    |
| read a file              | `cat f`, `less f`, `head -20 f`, `tail -f log` | `q` leaves `less`; `tail -f` follows a growing file       |
| find text                | `grep -rn "S-8" parking/`                      | `-r` recursive, `-n` line numbers, `-i` ignore case       |
| find files               | `find . -name '*.test.js'`                     | quotes keep the shell from expanding `*` early            |
| make, copy, move, remove | `mkdir -p a/b`, `cp`, `mv`, `rm`               | `rm` does not ask and there is no trash                   |
| which program will run   | `which node`                                   | the first match on `$PATH`                                |
| how do I use this        | `git --help`, `man ls`                         |                                                           |
| stop it                  | `Ctrl-C`                                       | `Ctrl-D` ends input; `:q!` leaves vim if you fell into it |
| that command again       | `Ctrl-R`, then type part of it                 | reverse history search; `↑` walks history                 |
| finish the word for me   | `Tab`                                          | twice to list the choices                                 |
| chain                    | `a && b`                                       | `b` runs only if `a` exited zero; `a ; b` runs both       |
| pipe                     | `git log --oneline | head -5`                  |                                                           |
| save output              | `npm test > out.txt 2>&1`                      |                                                           |

**Paths.** `~` is home, `.` is here, `..` is up one. A path starting with `/` is absolute; anything
else is relative to `pwd`. Quote paths with spaces: `cd "My Documents"`. And one trap that bites git
users on Macs: the default Mac filesystem is case-insensitive, so `Notes.md` and `notes.md` are the
same file to you and different files to git and to Linux. Name files in one case and keep it.

**Variables.** `NAME=value` sets one for this shell; `export NAME=value` sets one that programs you
start will inherit. `DATABASE_URL=... npm start` sets one for a single command. That last form is
how `parking/` is run outside Docker, and it is how a secret gets into a process without touching a
file (`1PASSWORD.md`).

### 9.4 Danger Will Robinson

- **`rm -rf $DIR`** with `DIR` unset is `rm -rf /`. Quote and check variables before deleting with
  them, or use a path that starts with `~/projects/`.
- **`curl … | sh`** runs whatever the server sent, as you. Download it first, read it, then run it.
  The installers in this sequence are fine; the habit is the problem.
- **`sudo`** means "as the administrator." If a command needs it and you do not know why, find out
  first. Nothing in a project directory should need it.
- **Spaces** split words. `git add my file.txt` adds two files, one of which does not exist.

### 9.5 When it goes wrong

| It says                         | It means                                 | Do                                                                  |
| ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `command not found`             | not on `$PATH`, or not installed         | `which`; install it; check the startup file exports `PATH`          |
| `No such file or directory`     | wrong working directory, or a typo       | `pwd`; `ls`; tab-complete the name instead of typing it             |
| `Permission denied`             | not yours, or not executable             | `ls -l` to see the owner and mode; `chmod +x script.sh`             |
| nothing happens, cursor blinks  | the program is waiting for input or hung | `Ctrl-C`; if it was waiting for input, that is what `Ctrl-D` is for |
| the screen is full of `~` lines | you are in `less` or `vim`               | `q`, or `Esc` then `:q!`                                            |
| `^M` at the ends of lines       | Windows line endings                     | `GIT.md` fixes this with one `.gitattributes` line                  |
| it is slow under WSL            | the project is under `/mnt/c`            | move it to `~/projects` on the Linux side                           |

### 9.6 Checklist

- [ ] A terminal opens and `echo $SHELL` names a shell you recognize.
- [ ] `~/projects` exists and is where projects go.
- [ ] `which git` prints a path.
- [ ] `code .` opens the current directory in an editor with a terminal pane.
- [ ] On Windows, the project is under the WSL home, not under `/mnt/c`.
- [ ] You can explain `|`, `>`, `2>&1`, and `$?` to a classmate.

### 9.7 In `parking/`

Every command in `CLAUDE.md` is a shell command. `npm run check` is two of them joined with `&&`,
which is why the layering check gates the tests: a nonzero exit code stops the chain.
`cli/check-layering.sh` is forty lines of plain `sh` and worth reading as a first script — notice
`set -eu` at the top, which makes the script stop on the first error and refuse to use an unset
variable, which is exactly the `rm -rf $DIR` protection above, applied to itself.

### 9.8 Resources

- The Missing Semester of Your CS Education (MIT) — the shell, the editor, and git, in a week.
- `man bash`, or `man zsh`, when you are ready for the full story. Not before.

## 10. Git

Git is the version-control tool Linus Torvalds wrote to manage large federated projects like the
Linux kernel. It is now used for far more than code: server configuration, documentation, and web
content are all problems that benefit from a history you can go back to. In this course it is also
the mechanism of ownership — a commit on `main` is signed by a person who has read it.

- **The fear it retires:** "I can't get back to when it worked." And, signed: "nobody vouched for
  this code."
- **The fence you prove:** `ssh -T git@github.com` greets you by name, and a commit you made shows
  **Verified** on GitHub.
- **Before this:** `SHELL.md`
- **After this:** `1PASSWORD.md` — you have just created two secrets that need a home

### 10.1 The model

A repository is a graph of snapshots. Each node is a complete state of the project — source, tests,
build scripts, images — and each arrow points at what came before. A branch is a name for the newest
node on one line of work. Merging joins two lines.

```
             iss32:  o──o──o
                    /        \
  main:  o──o──o──o───o───o───o──▶   (each o is a commit; a name like `main` points at the newest)
```

Locally, git keeps three things you move changes between, and most confusion is not knowing which
one a command touches:

```
  working tree ──git add──▶ index (staged) ──git commit──▶ history (HEAD) ──git push──▶ remote (origin)
  the files you edit        the next commit's contents      what is recorded            GitHub's copy
                                                                           ◀──git pull──
```

**Danger Will Robinson.** Many tutorials show you how to make an isolated repository, and it is
often a checkbox in an IDE. This is a **bad** idea, because there is safety in numbers, and you will
be sad one day when your system does not boot and all your work is lost. A repository has a remote,
or it is not finished.

#### Things to remember

- **Source goes in.** Code, tests, build scripts, images, sounds, and the documents that say what
  the code is for.

- **Build artifacts, secrets, and minutiae stay out.** Executables, libraries, `node_modules`,
  precompiled headers; API keys and passwords; the IDE's record of which windows are open.

- **Branches track issues, not people.** `db`, `ui`, `iss32` — not `alice` and `bob`. Bob might be
  sick and Alice has to step in. Git already records who made each change; the flow of work is about
  resolving issues.

- **Experiments are not on `main`.** `main` is a sequence of merges from branches of code that
  compiles and passes more and more tests.

- **Git is an elephant. It never forgets.** Once something is pushed, getting rid of it means
  rewriting history, force-pushing, and every collaborator re-cloning — and on a public repository,
  forks and caches mean you cannot be sure it is gone at all. So:

  - **Do not** `git add .` or use wildcard adds. You will add build artifacts that slow everyone
    down and create binary merge conflicts. Add files by name.
  - **Do not** add build artifacts. Large, useless to version control, and a conflict for everyone.
  - **Do not** add secrets. Use a password manager (`1PASSWORD.md`). If a secret does get pushed,
    **rotate it first** — revoke the key, issue a new one — before spending a minute scrubbing
    history, because the pushed value was compromised the moment it landed.
  - **Do not** add IDE minutiae. Removing them breaks the IDE; a conflict in them means you cannot
    use the IDE to fix it. A `.gitignore` says which files git should stop mentioning.

Most of this will not mean much until you have been bitten once. Read it again then.

### 10.2 Once per machine

**Get git.** `SHELL.md` installed it: `xcode-select --install` on a Mac, `apt-get install git` on
Ubuntu and WSL. `git --version` confirms. Learn the command line even if you like GUI tools: you
will eventually decide it is faster, and every answer on the internet is a command, not a click.

**Sign up for GitHub.** Not with your campus email. GitHub should follow you into your career, so
use a permanent professional address you would be willing to show an employer. The free tier gives
unlimited public and private repositories with unlimited collaborators; the [student developer
pack](https://education.github.com/pack) adds paid tools while you are a student, and expires when
you stop being one, so do not build anything you depend on around it.

Turn on two-factor authentication now, not when it blocks you, and put the recovery codes in your
password manager (`1PASSWORD.md`). Every term somebody locks themselves out of the account holding
all their coursework, and there is very little anyone can do about it.

**D1. Tell git who you are.** Your real name, and an email that is verified on your GitHub account;
otherwise your commits will not link to your profile, which matters when someone looks you up to
decide whether to interview you. If you would rather not have your address in every public commit,
GitHub issues a private `noreply` address under Settings → Emails; use that here.

```sh
git config --global user.name  "Jane Doe"
git config --global user.email "jane@example.com"
```

**D2. Make a key pair.** Press Enter through the prompts. If it says the key already exists, answer
**n** — you do not want to overwrite the one you have.

```sh
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "jane@example.com"
```

This creates `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` (private — never share, never commit) and `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`
(public — the half you hand out).

**D3. Give GitHub the public half, twice.** Copy it to the clipboard:

```sh
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub | pbcopy                 # mac
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub | clip.exe               # windows (git-bash or WSL)
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub | xclip -selection c     # linux (apt-get install xclip)
```

Then GitHub → your avatar → Settings → *SSH and GPG keys* → *New SSH key*. Add it **once as an
Authentication Key** (so you can push) and **once more as a Signing Key** (so your commits show as
Verified). Name each for the machine it lives on: "laptop", "lab-3".

**D3b. Check it.** Before cloning anything:

```sh
ssh -T git@github.com
```

The first time it asks you to confirm GitHub's fingerprint; type `yes`. Success looks like a
refusal: *Hi jane! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access.* If
you see `Permission denied (publickey)` instead, go back to D3; every later command will fail in a
more confusing way.

If it hangs forever, your network is blocking port 22 — some campus and corporate networks do.
GitHub takes SSH over 443; put this in `~/.ssh/config`:

```
Host github.com
  Hostname ssh.github.com
  Port 443
```

**D4. Sign your commits.** This repository requires it (`CONTRIBUTING.md`), and it is the same key.
Four lines, once per machine:

```sh
git config --global gpg.format ssh
git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
git config --global commit.gpgsign true
git config --global tag.gpgsign true
```

To *verify* signatures locally, git needs a list of trusted keys; this repository keeps one at
`.github/allowed_signers`, and `CONTRIBUTING.md` shows the per-repository line that points git at
it. Add yourself to that file in the format it shows. Then `git log --show-signature -1` after your
next commit should say *Good "git" signature*, and GitHub will show **Verified** beside it.

**D5. Pick where projects live.** `~/projects`, per `SHELL.md`.

### 10.3 Once per repository

Two flavors. `<user>` is your GitHub username; `<repo>` is the repository name, in whatever
convention your professor requires.

**Clone, GitHub → local.** Easiest, and right whenever the files do not already exist on your
machine. Create the repository on GitHub (the `+` by your avatar), **non-empty**: include a README,
a LICENSE, and a `.gitignore` for your language. Then, from your projects directory:

```sh
cd ~/projects
git clone git@github.com:<user>/<repo>.git
```

**Push, local → GitHub.** When the project already exists on your machine. Create the repository on
GitHub **empty** — no README, no nothing. Then, inside the project directory:

```sh
git init .
git add <file1> <file2> ...        # by name; no wildcards
git commit -m "initial commit"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin git@github.com:<user>/<repo>.git
git push -u origin main
```

**Use SSH, not HTTPS.** HTTPS with a token is not insecure; it is friction, and friction is what
kills the habit. The address from GitHub's *Code* button, SSH tab, looks like
`git@github.com:<user>/<repo>.git`.

**Two files in the first commit.**

- `.gitignore` — the patterns git should stop mentioning: `node_modules/`, build output, `.env`, the
  IDE's state. GitHub's language templates are a good start; this repository's is short and
  commented.
- `.gitattributes` with one line, `* text=auto`. Windows ends lines differently from Mac and Linux,
  and in a mixed team that shows up as a diff claiming you changed all four hundred lines of a file
  you barely touched. This line makes git normalize line endings in the repository and hand each
  person the flavor their system expects.

**Do not create a repository inside a repository.** IDEs notice they are in a git-managed directory;
if one offers to initialize a new one, say no.

### 10.4 Every day

**See what changed.** `git status` lists files changed since the last commit; `git diff` shows the
changes; `git diff --staged` shows what the next commit will contain. If `status` keeps showing
files you do not want, that is what `.gitignore` is for.

**Add and commit.** Name the files. Commit with a message that says *why*, and, in this repository,
the requirement ID:

```sh
git add contract/signing.js contract/signing.test.js
git commit -m "S-8: refuse a field containing the separator"
```

This only affects the local repository. Almost always follow it with `git push`.

**Push early. Push often.** Your code takes up very little space and you will miss it if you lose
it. A pushed commit is a backup you can get back to; on your own branch it is not a decision you
have to defend.

**Give and take.** If you are not the only one pushing to a branch, sync the other way too: `git
pull`.

**Push rejected.** Sooner or later: `! [rejected] main -> main (fetch first)`. Nothing is broken.
The remote has commits you do not, because somebody else pushed or you pushed from another machine,
and git will not let you overwrite what you have not seen. Bring theirs down, then send yours up:
`git pull`, then `git push`. If git asks how to reconcile divergent branches, tell it once,
globally, to merge: `git config --global pull.rebase false`. **Never** fix a rejected push with `git
push --force`: it does exactly what it says and throws away commits you had not seen, which is
somebody else's afternoon.

#### Branches

`main` is what GitHub creates now; older repositories say `master`. `git branch` tells you which you
are in. It is easy to forget which branch you are on and branch from the wrong one, so start from
`main`, fresh:

```sh
git switch main             # make sure you are on main   (older git: git checkout main)
git pull                    # get the latest from origin
git switch -c iss32         # create iss32 and switch to it (older git: git checkout -b iss32)
git push -u origin iss32    # publish it and remember the pairing; once per branch
```

`git branch -a` lists every branch, local and remote. Commit and push before switching branches. Git
will sometimes let you switch with uncommitted changes sitting there, but "sometimes" is not a rule
you can build a habit on, and half-switched work is how people lose an afternoon.

Deleting a branch is easy — `git branch -d iss32` locally, `git push origin --delete iss32` remotely
— and usually unnecessary; a dead branch costs nothing. Deleting a *commit* that has been pushed is
the elephant again.

#### Merging

Merging does not end either branch. To bring `main` into your issue branch, which you should do
often so that your eventual pull request is clean:

```sh
git switch main && git pull        # get main current
git switch iss32                   # back to your work
git merge main                     # bring main in
git push
```

A good policy: merge `main` into the issue branch first; when the issue branch has all of `main`'s
changes and passes all the tests, *then* merge the issue branch into `main` — or, on a team, open a
pull request, which is the same merge proposed rather than performed (`GITHUB-ISSUES.md`).

#### When a merge stops with a conflict

A conflict means two branches changed the same lines and git will not guess which you meant. It is a
normal part of merging, not a sign something went wrong: the merge pauses and waits. `git status`
lists the conflicted files under *Unmerged paths*, and those are the only files you touch.

Inside one, the disputed region is marked:

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
what your branch says
=======
what the branch you are merging says
>>>>>>> main
```

Make those lines read the way the file should finally read, and delete all three marker lines. In VS
Code the file shows the two versions as colored blocks with links above them — *Accept Current*,
*Accept Incoming*, *Accept Both*, *Compare Changes* — and the Source Control pane lists every
conflicted file so you can watch the list shrink. For anything more tangled than a line, *Compare
Changes* opens a three-way view that is much easier to think in than raw markers.

**Read the result before you move on.** Accepting one side is a decision about what the program
should do, and the buttons make it fast enough to click through without reading. A file with both
sides accepted often compiles fine and is still wrong.

When the file reads correctly: `git add` it to mark it resolved, repeat until nothing is unmerged,
`git commit` (git writes the message), `git push`. Two escape hatches: `git merge --abort` puts you
back exactly where you started, and `git checkout --merge <file>` restores the markers in one file
if you mangled your edits. The first is the important one: you are never trapped in a merge.

#### Undo, by how far it went

| The change is…                         | Undo with                          | Notes                                                   |
| -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| in the working tree, not staged        | `git restore <file>`               | gone for good; it was never recorded                    |
| staged, not committed                  | `git restore --staged <file>`      | unstages; the edit stays in the file                    |
| committed, not pushed, wrong message   | `git commit --amend`               | rewrites the last commit; fine before pushing           |
| committed, not pushed, wrong contents  | `git reset --soft HEAD~1`          | uncommits, keeps the changes staged                     |
| committed and pushed                   | `git revert <sha>`                 | a new commit that undoes it; history intact             |
| lost — "I had it a minute ago"         | `git reflog`                       | the elephant working for you: every `HEAD` git has seen |
| in the way — "I need a clean tree now" | `git stash`, later `git stash pop` | a shelf, not a branch; do not leave things on it        |

The line between the rows is *pushed*. Above it, rewriting is fine. Below it, add a commit instead.

### 10.5 Danger Will Robinson

- `git push --force` on a branch anyone else uses.
- `git add .` — see the elephant.
- A commit you cannot explain. In this repository your signature says *I have read this and I stand
  behind it*, and an agent's draft you did not read is exactly what the rule exists to catch.
- `git checkout` of a branch with uncommitted work you cared about.

### 10.6 Checklist

- [ ] `ssh -T git@github.com` greets you by name.
- [ ] Two-factor is on, and the recovery codes are in your password manager.
- [ ] `git config --global -l` shows your name, a verified email, and `commit.gpgsign=true`.
- [ ] Your public key is on GitHub as both an authentication key and a signing key.
- [ ] A commit you made shows **Verified** on GitHub, and `git log --show-signature -1` agrees.
- [ ] The repository has `.gitignore` and `.gitattributes`, and has a remote.
- [ ] You have resolved one merge conflict on purpose and read the result.

### 10.7 In `parking/`

`CONTRIBUTING.md` is the policy this document sets up: every commit on `main` is signed, the
signature is SSH, and `.github/allowed_signers` is the registry of humans — the same structure as
the device registry in `parking/DESIGN.md`, one layer up. Commit messages name the requirement ID
(`S-8`, `C-4`) so that `git log --grep S-8` walks from the history to the sentence that demanded the
change. And `.gitignore` there refuses `*.key` and `*.pem` while allowing `*.pub`, which is
requirement `I-7` enforced at the boundary git controls.

### 10.8 Resources

- [Learn Git Branching](https://learngitbranching.js.org/) — the graph, interactively. An hour well
  spent before your first merge.
- [Pro Git](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2) — the book, free. Chapters 2 and 3 are the daily
  commands; chapter 7 is what to read when you are ready to rewrite history on purpose.
- [Oh Shit, Git!?!](https://ohshitgit.com/) — the undo table above, in the voice you will be in when
  you need it.
- Udacity's *Version Control with Git* and *Shell Workshop* — free, short, and paced for beginners.

## 11. 1Password

You now own secrets: an SSH private key, two-factor recovery codes, and — the first time a project
talks to any service — an API key. A secret has one property that nothing else you handle has: once
it is in the wrong place, you cannot get it back. This is the tool that keeps secrets out of files,
out of chat, and out of the repository, while still getting them into the programs that need them.

- **The fear it retires:** "A secret is in the repo." And: "I'm locked out of the account with all
  my work in it."
- **The fence you prove:** `parking/` runs with `JWT_SECRET` injected by `op run`, nothing secret in
  any file, and your GitHub recovery codes are in the vault.
- **Before this:** `GIT.md`
- **After this:** `GITHUB-ISSUES.md`

Why this product: its developer tooling can put a secret into a program's environment at run time so
that it never touches a file, it has an SSH agent, and it has not lost its customers' vaults. Do not
use LastPass; its customer vaults themselves were stolen in the 2022 breach. Any manager with the
first two properties will do; the habits below are the point.

### 11.1 The model

```
  vault ── items ── fields            the app (unlock with one password + a secret key)
    │                                  the browser extension (fills logins; generates passwords)
    │                                  the CLI, `op` (reads fields into a shell or a process)
    │                                  the SSH agent (signs with keys that never leave the vault)
    ▼
  repository: NO secrets.
  a template file: JWT_SECRET=op://Development/parking/jwt-secret     ← a reference, not a value
    │
    └── op run --env-file=.env.template -- npm start   ──▶  the process sees JWT_SECRET=<value>
                                                             and nothing on disk ever did
```

Three ideas:

- **A secret is a value that lives in exactly one place**, the vault, and is *referenced* everywhere
  else. A reference like `op://vault/item/field` is safe to commit; it is an address, not a key.
- **The environment is the delivery route.** Programs read secrets from environment variables
  (`SHELL.md`); the manager sets them for one process and nothing else sees them.
- **Your email account is the master key to everything else**, because every "forgot password" flow
  goes through it. It gets the strongest password, hardware or app two-factor, and its own recovery
  codes in the vault.

### 11.2 Once per machine

1. **Install the app and the browser extension.** Create the account with a long master password you
   will actually type, and save the *Emergency Kit* — the PDF with your secret key — somewhere that
   is not this machine. Without the secret key, a new device cannot join, and support cannot help
   you.

2. **Install the CLI** (`op`), and turn on *Settings → Developer → Integrate with 1Password CLI* so
   that `op` unlocks with the app instead of asking for the password every time. `op signin` once,
   then `op whoami` to confirm.

3. **Turn on the SSH agent** (*Settings → Developer → Use the SSH agent*) and either import the key
   you made in `GIT.md` into the vault as an *SSH Key* item, or generate a new one there and add its
   public half to GitHub. Then tell SSH to ask the agent:

   ```
   # ~/.ssh/config
   Host *
     IdentityAgent "~/Library/Group Containers/2BUA8C4S2C.com.1password/t/agent.sock"   # mac
   # linux: IdentityAgent ~/.1password/agent.sock
   ```

   `ssh-add -l` should now list the key, and `ssh -T git@github.com` should still greet you. On
   Windows the agent speaks through the OpenSSH named pipe, and using it from WSL takes a bridge; if
   that is friction, keep the key file in WSL and store a *copy* of the key in the vault as the
   backup it should have anyway.

4. **Move your existing secrets in.** GitHub login and its two-factor recovery codes. Your email
   account and its codes. The SSH key. Anything currently in a notes file, a text message, or a
   screenshot of a QR code.

### 11.3 Once per repository

1. **`.env` is in `.gitignore`.** Check before anything else. `git status` must never show it.

2. **Commit a template, not a value.** `.env.template` (or `.env.example`) holds references:

   ```
   DATABASE_URL=postgres://parking_user:parking_pass@localhost:5432/parking
   JWT_SECRET=op://Development/parking/jwt-secret
   ```

   The database line is not a secret here — it is the local Docker demo, and `docker-compose.yml`
   says so in plain text. The JWT secret is. That distinction is a decision; make it on purpose and
   write it down.

3. **Create the item.** In the *Development* vault, an item named `parking` with a field
   `jwt-secret`, generated by the app, long, never typed by a human.

4. **Run through the manager.**

   ```sh
   cd parking/app
   op run --env-file=../.env.template -- npm start
   ```

   `op` resolves every `op://` reference, sets the variables for that one process, and forgets them
   when it exits. `op read "op://Development/parking/jwt-secret"` prints one value when you need to
   see it, which should be rare.

5. **Share by vault, not by message.** A teammate who needs the secret gets access to the shared
   vault. A secret pasted into chat is in that chat's history forever, on servers you do not
   control.

### 11.4 Every day

- The extension fills logins and generates a new password for every new site. You should not know
  any of your passwords except the master one.
- *Watchtower* tells you which saved passwords have appeared in a breach; rotate those.
- When a project needs a new key: generate it in the service, paste it into a vault item **once**,
  reference it from the template, close the tab. It never goes in a file.
- When a secret must be rotated — a teammate leaves, a laptop is lost — change the vault item and
  every process picks it up on its next start. That is the payoff for never copying it anywhere.

### 11.5 Danger Will Robinson

- **A secret that was pushed is compromised**, however briefly it was there. Rotate it first —
  revoke, reissue — then, if you must, scrub history with `git filter-repo`, knowing that forks and
  caches may still have it.
- **`.env` in the repository.** The single most common way a key leaks. The `.gitignore` line is not
  optional, and `git add .` is how it gets bypassed (`GIT.md`).
- **Secrets in a Docker image.** `ENV JWT_SECRET=…` in a Dockerfile, or a build argument, is in the
  image's layers forever, and anyone who can pull the image can read it (`DOCKER.md`).
- **Secrets in a prompt.** Pasting a key into a chat with an agent sends it to a third party
  (`AGENT.md`).
- **Secrets in logs.** `L-7` in `parking/REQUIREMENTS.md`: credentials, private keys, and tokens are
  never logged; fingerprints and subjects are.
- **One password reused.** The breach of a site you forgot about becomes the breach of your email,
  and your email is the master key.

### 11.6 When it goes wrong

| Symptom                                                | Cause                                    | Do                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| a key or token is in a commit                          | added by wildcard, or `.env` not ignored | rotate it now; then clean history; then fix `.gitignore`                                                        |
| `ssh -T` stopped greeting you after enabling the agent | SSH is asking the wrong agent            | `ssh-add -l`; check `IdentityAgent` in `~/.ssh/config`; `echo $SSH_AUTH_SOCK`                                   |
| `op run` says it cannot resolve a reference            | vault, item, or field name is wrong      | `op item get parking --vault Development` and read the field names                                              |
| locked out of GitHub after a phone change              | two-factor with no recovery codes        | the codes are in the vault — that is why they are there; if not, GitHub's recovery process is slow and may fail |
| a new laptop cannot unlock the vault                   | no secret key                            | the Emergency Kit; this is the one thing you cannot reset                                                       |

### 11.7 Checklist

- [ ] The Emergency Kit is stored somewhere that is not this machine.
- [ ] GitHub login, two-factor recovery codes, and the email account are items in the vault.
- [ ] `ssh-add -l` lists a key served by the agent, or the key file is backed up in the vault.
- [ ] `.env` is in `.gitignore`; `.env.template` with `op://` references is committed.
- [ ] `parking/` starts with `op run`, and no secret value is in any file in the repository.
- [ ] You know the rotate-first rule and could say it from memory.

### 11.8 In `parking/`

`I-7` says no credential, private key, or signing key is committed or baked into an image; public
keys and trust anchors may be. `I-2` says a device's private key is generated on the device and
never leaves it — the same one-place rule, applied to a sensor. `L-7` keeps secrets out of logs. And
`app/index.js` falls back to `dev-secret` when `JWT_SECRET` is unset, with a warning: a deliberate
falsehood for a demo, and exactly the kind of default that reaches production when nobody has set up
the route this document describes.

### 11.9 Resources

- 1Password's developer documentation: *Secret references*, *`op run`*, and *SSH agent* are the
  three pages this document is built on.
- `git filter-repo` — the tool for rewriting history when you must, and its README on why you
  usually should not.

## 12. GitHub Issues and Pull Requests

Git records *what* changed. This is the layer that records *why*, *who is on it*, and *whether
anyone else looked*. An issue is a unit of work; a branch is named for it; a pull request proposes
the merge; a review approves it; the merge closes the issue. One loop, and every step leaves a
record someone can find in a month.

- **The fear it retires:** "Nobody knows what is being worked on, or why this change exists, or
  whether anyone read it."
- **The fence you prove:** An issue closed automatically by a merged pull request that names it,
  with a review approval and a green check on it.
- **Before this:** `1PASSWORD.md`
- **After this:** `GITHUB-ACTIONS.md` — the green check is what that one supplies

### 12.1 The model

```
  issue #32 ──▶ branch iss32 ──▶ commits ──▶ pull request ──▶ review + checks ──▶ merge ──▶ closed
  the why       the where        the what     the proposal     the evidence        the record
```

**Branches track issues, not people** (`GIT.md`). The issue number is the thread that ties the
branch, the commits, the pull request, and the conversation together, and `Closes #32` in the pull
request is what closes the loop by machine rather than by memory.

Three more objects, and what each is for:

| Object        | What it is                                        | Here                                                 |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Label         | a tag on an issue: `bug`, `requirement`, `S`, `C` | the requirement section, so `S` issues can be listed |
| Milestone     | a named date that issues belong to                | the iteration (`docs/TEAM-AND-CLIENT.md`)            |
| Project board | columns of issues: to do, doing, done             | `QUEUE`, held by the Queue role                      |

### 12.2 Once per repository

1. **Protect `main`.** *Settings → Branches → Add rule* for `main`: require a pull request before
   merging, require status checks to pass, require signed commits, and do not allow force pushes.
   After this a direct push to `main` is refused no matter how correct the merge was, which is the
   point.
2. **Decide the merge method**, once, in *Settings → General → Pull Requests*. Merge commits keep
   every commit and add one; squash collapses the branch into one commit; rebase replays them. Pick
   one so the history reads one way. Whatever you pick: **merging in the web UI produces a commit
   signed by GitHub's key, not yours.** This repository's signature check (`CONTRIBUTING.md`) trusts
   only keys in `.github/allowed_signers`, so the merge that lands on `main` is done locally, with
   your key, and pushed — the pull request still carries the review.
3. **Add templates.** `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` with the four headings from
   `CONTRIBUTING.md`: what changed, which requirement IDs, how you verified it, what you
   deliberately left out. `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` with two forms: a bug (steps to reproduce,
   expected, actual) and a requirement (the observable sentence, the ID, the done criterion).
4. **Create the labels** you will actually filter by. Fewer is better; a label nobody filters by is
   noise.

### 12.3 Every day

#### Writing an issue

An issue is a *what* and a *why*, in a form that can be closed:

- **Title as a verb phrase.** "Mark a lot stale when `age_ms` exceeds the threshold," not
  "staleness."
- **The pain, then the observable done criterion.** What happens today, what must be true when it is
  fixed, which requirement ID. "Done when `T-2`'s stuck-sensor test passes and the driver view shows
  the age."
- **Not a design.** "Add a `stale` column" is a design; the issue says what must be observable, and
  the pull request says how (`AGILE_VS_WATERFALL.md`, section on requirement versus design).
- **A bug report is a reproduction.** Exact steps, exact values, exact output. A bug you cannot
  reproduce is a rumor, and `T-1` — deterministic sequences, exact asserted values — is what makes a
  reproduction possible to write.
- **Assign it** when someone starts, not before. An issue with an assignee and no branch for a week
  is the stand-up's "blocked — since when."

#### Opening a pull request

```sh
git switch main && git pull
git switch -c iss32
# ... work, commit by name, push early ...
git push -u origin iss32
```

GitHub offers a *Compare & pull request* button right after the push. Fill the template. Put `Closes
#32` in the description. Mark it a **draft** if it is not ready for review; a draft says "look if
you like, do not approve yet."

Keep it to **one concern.** Reviewer attention is the scarce resource, and a bundled diff spends it
on separating things that should never have been joined. If the change touches two requirements,
that is two pull requests. Merge `main` into your branch first (`GIT.md`) so the diff shows only
your change.

#### Reviewing

The reviewer asks three questions, in order (`CONTRIBUTING.md`):

1. Does it do what the requirement says, and does the test prove it?
2. Could a student read this in a month and explain why it is here?
3. What does it make harder later?

Comment on lines, not in general. *Approve*, *Request changes*, or *Comment* — and say which
question the comment is about. As the author, respond to every comment, even with "done," so the
reviewer can see the thread close. Push more commits to the same branch; the pull request updates.

**Read the whole diff.** The one line you skipped is the one that was generated, or pasted, or
merged wrong. If you cannot explain a line, it does not go in; that rule applies to reviewers as
much as authors.

#### Merging

When the checks are green and the review is approved:

```sh
git switch iss32 && git pull
git switch main && git pull           # main may have moved
git merge iss32                       # signed with your key
git push                              # the PR shows Merged; #32 closes
```

Then leave the branch alone or delete it; it costs nothing either way.

### 12.4 Danger Will Robinson

- **`git push --force` to a branch with an open pull request.** It rewrites what the reviewer
  already read.
- **A pull request nobody can review in one sitting.** Three hundred lines from an agent is not a
  pull request; it is a request that someone else take ownership of something you did not read.
- **Issues used as chat.** Decisions go in the description or in the documents; a forty-comment
  thread is where decisions go to be lost.
- **Closing an issue by hand** when the pull request should have. If it did not close, the
  description did not say `Closes #32`, and the link between the change and its reason is gone.

### 12.5 When it goes wrong

| Symptom                                                      | Cause                                         | Do                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| "This branch has conflicts that must be resolved"            | `main` moved under you                        | `git merge main` into your branch, resolve, push (`GIT.md`)                                                              |
| the check is red                                             | the tests fail on a machine that is not yours | read the log from the first red step; reproduce with the same command (`GITHUB-ACTIONS.md`)                              |
| you committed to `main` by accident                          | forgot to branch                              | before pushing: `git switch -c iss32` takes the commits with you; then `git switch main && git reset --hard origin/main` |
| the merge was refused: "required status check" or "unsigned" | protection is doing its job                   | fix the cause; do not ask an admin to bypass it                                                                          |
| two people did the same task                                 | no assignee, or no board                      | the Queue role's cursor exists to prevent this; use it                                                                   |

### 12.6 Checklist

- [ ] `main` is protected: pull request required, checks required, signed commits required, no force
      pushes.
- [ ] The merge method is decided and written down.
- [ ] Pull request and issue templates exist and match `CONTRIBUTING.md`.
- [ ] Every branch is named for an issue.
- [ ] Every pull request says what changed, which IDs, how verified, and what was left out.
- [ ] You have opened, reviewed, and merged one pull request that closed its issue by itself.

### 12.7 In `parking/`

The seven unbuilt components are seven issues waiting to be opened, each with its README as the
description and its requirement IDs as the done criterion. The `Migration` note in `REQUIREMENTS.md`
— retire the push endpoint and the `sensor` role when the collector lands — is an issue with a
stated trigger. And `CONTRIBUTING.md`'s pull-request section is the template above, already written:
one concern, four headings, three reviewer questions.

### 12.8 Resources

- GitHub's own documentation on *branch protection rules*, *linking a pull request to an issue*, and
  *issue and pull request templates* — short, and they move the buttons, so prefer these to
  screenshots.
- `gh` — GitHub's command-line tool. `gh pr create`, `gh pr checks`, `gh issue list` do everything
  above without leaving the terminal, and `gh pr checkout 32` fetches a teammate's branch for review
  in one line.

## 13. GitHub Actions

Continuous integration is the idiot light with a URL. Every push is built and tested on a machine
that is not yours, and the result is one green or red mark on the pull request and one badge on the
README. It retires two fears at once — "it works on my machine" and "nobody ran the tests" — and it
is worth trusting only when it runs the same command you do.

- **The fear it retires:** "It works on my machine." "Nobody ran the tests before merging."
- **The fence you prove:** A green run on every push to your fork, running `npm run check` from
  `parking/`, with the badge in the README.
- **Before this:** `GITHUB-ISSUES.md`
- **After this:** `DOCKER.md`

### 13.1 The model

```
  event (push, pull_request, schedule, manual)
    └─▶ workflow   (.github/workflows/check.yml)
          └─▶ job(s)   (each on a fresh runner: a virtual machine GitHub starts and throws away)
                └─▶ steps   (a shell command, or an action someone published)
                      └─▶ log, and an exit code   ──▶  ✓ or ✗ on the commit, the PR, and the badge
```

Three things to hold onto:

- **The runner is a stranger's machine.** Nothing on it is yours: no global installs, no `.env`, no
  `~/.ssh`. Whatever the job needs, a step has to put there. That is the feature — it is what makes
  "works on my machine" impossible to hide.
- **The exit code is the verdict.** A step that exits nonzero fails the job. `npm run check` is
  already shaped for this (`SHELL.md`).
- **The workflow file is code**, in the repository, reviewed like anything else. Changing it is a
  pull request.

### 13.2 Once per repository

Create `.github/workflows/check.yml`. This is the workflow `CONTRIBUTING.md` describes for this
repository, with the parts that exist today:

```yaml
name: check

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:            # a "Run workflow" button, for when you want to run it by hand

permissions:
  contents: read                # least privilege: this workflow never writes to the repository

concurrency:
  group: check-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true      # a second push makes the first run's answer irrelevant

jobs:
  tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: parking
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5      # use the current major; the log warns when one is retired
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - run: npm run check                # the same command you run: layering rule, then tests

  signatures:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0                  # the whole history, so the range below exists
      - run: git config gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile .github/allowed_signers
      - run: |
          git log --format='%H %G?' origin/${{ github.base_ref }}..HEAD |
            awk '$2 != "G" { print "unsigned or untrusted: " $1; bad = 1 } END { exit bad }'

  integration:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: parking
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: docker compose up --build -d
      - name: wait for the app                         # the power-on self test, from outside
        run: |
          for i in $(seq 1 30); do
            curl -fsS http://localhost:3000/api/lots > /dev/null && exit 0
            sleep 2
          done
          docker compose logs; exit 1
      - run: curl -fsS http://localhost:3000/api/lots | head -c 400
      - if: always()
        run: docker compose down -v
```

Two of the three jobs are exactly the checks `CONTRIBUTING.md` lists; the third stands in for
`parkctl conform --all --json` until `parkctl` exists. When it does, replace the `curl` line with
the conformance command and the job is done — the exit code is already the interface.

**The badge.** In `README.md`:

```
[![check](https://github.com/<user>/<repo>/actions/workflows/check.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/<user>/<repo>/actions/workflows/check.yml)
```

**Required checks.** In the branch protection rule (`GITHUB-ISSUES.md`), add `tests` and
`signatures` as required. Now a pull request cannot merge red.

### 13.3 Every day

- **Push, then look.** The *Actions* tab, or the ✓/✗ beside the commit. Red means read the log,
  starting at the first red step, not the last.
- **Reproduce locally with the same command.** If CI ran `npm run check`, run `npm run check`. If it
  passes locally and fails in CI, the difference is the environment, and `DOCKER.md` and
  `PACKAGES.md` are about exactly that difference.
- **Keep the workflow the same as your script.** If the build step is `./build.sh` in both places
  there is no second recipe to drift. A workflow full of steps that nobody runs locally is a
  workflow nobody can debug.

#### Platforms

Building for a platform and running on it are different tests. A matrix runs the same job on several
runners, and `fail-fast: false` keeps the others going when one breaks, because the interesting
question is always *which* platforms broke:

```yaml
  tests:
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, ubuntu-24.04-arm, macos-latest, windows-latest]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
```

`ubuntu-24.04-arm` is a real `arm64` machine, which is how the container nuance in `DOCKER.md` gets
tested rather than assumed.

#### Secrets in a workflow

*Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions.* A secret is exposed to a step only as `${{
secrets.NAME }}`, is masked in the log, and is **not** available to pull requests from forks. Never
`echo` one. Prefer not to need one: the tests in this repository need no secret at all, and that is
a design property worth keeping.

### 13.4 Danger Will Robinson

- **`pull_request_target` with a checkout of the pull request's code.** That event runs with the
  base repository's secrets; checking out and executing a stranger's branch under it hands them your
  secrets. Use `pull_request` unless you know exactly why not.
- **Untrusted text inside `${{ }}` in a `run:` step.** `run: echo "${{ github.event.issue.title }}"`
  is a shell injection; a title containing `$(curl …)` runs it. Pass such values through `env:` and
  quote the variable: `env: TITLE: ${{ … }}` then `run: echo "$TITLE"`.
- **`permissions: write-all`**, or no `permissions:` block at all, which can default to more than
  you meant.
- **An unpinned action.** `uses: someone/action@main` runs whatever is on `main` today, as you. Pin
  a major at least; pin a commit SHA if the action is not from GitHub itself.
- **A path-filtered workflow made a required check.** If it never starts for a commit outside its
  paths, the pull request reads *pending* forever.

### 13.5 When it goes wrong

| Symptom                                       | Cause                                                                               | Do                                                                                         |
| --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| green locally, red in CI                      | the environment differs: Node version, a global, `.env`                             | pin the version in `setup-node`; remove the global; the runner has no `.env` — good        |
| red locally, green in CI                      | CI is not running what you think                                                    | read the workflow: is the working directory right? is the step actually running the tests? |
| red on Wednesday with no commit since Tuesday | something floated: a dependency, `ubuntu-latest`, an action major                   | `PACKAGES.md`: the lock file; pin the runner image; read the log's first red line          |
| the badge says "no status"                    | the workflow file name in the URL is wrong, or the workflow has never run on `main` | check the file name; push to `main` once                                                   |
| "resource not accessible by integration"      | `permissions` too narrow for a step                                                 | grant only the one permission that step needs                                              |
| the run is pending forever                    | a required check whose workflow did not start                                       | the path-filter trap above                                                                 |

### 13.6 Checklist

- [ ] `.github/workflows/check.yml` exists, runs `npm run check`, and is green on `main`.
- [ ] The workflow runs the same command you run by hand.
- [ ] `permissions:` is present and minimal; every job has `timeout-minutes`; actions are pinned.
- [ ] The badge is in the README and reflects `main`.
- [ ] `tests` and `signatures` are required checks on `main`.
- [ ] You have read one red log to its first red line and fixed the cause, not the symptom.

### 13.7 In `parking/`

`CONTRIBUTING.md` names three checks — signatures, conformance, integration — and says *anything
that is merely a convention is not a policy*. At this writing no workflow file exists in the
repository, so the checks are a convention. The file above is what turns them into a policy; adding
it is a pull request, and the first time it goes red on a real change is the first time the badge
means something.

### 13.8 Resources

- GitHub's *Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions* — the reference for every key used above.
- GitHub's *Security hardening for GitHub Actions* — the source of the Danger list, at length.
- The languages course repository's workflows — a six-platform matrix and a container build, both
  small enough to read in one sitting.

## 14. Docker

A container is one machine, described in a file, that anyone can start. It retires the other half of
"it works on my machine" — the half about what is installed — and it gives you the thing every test
suite needs most: one command back to a known state.

- **The fear it retires:** "It works on my machine." "I can't get back to a clean state."
- **The fence you prove:** From a clean clone, `docker compose up --build` serves
  `http://localhost:3000`; `docker compose down -v` and `up` again gives the seed state; and you can
  say which architecture the image was built for.
- **Before this:** `GITHUB-ACTIONS.md`
- **After this:** `PACKAGES.md`

### 14.1 The model

```
  Dockerfile ──build──▶ image ──run──▶ container ──▶ a process in its own filesystem and network
  (a recipe)            (immutable,     (one running    │
                         layered)        copy; cheap;   ├── volume:  state that outlives the container
                                         disposable)    ├── port:    host:3000 → container:3000
                                                        └── network: compose makes `db` a hostname
```

Four nouns, and the mistakes are mostly confusing two of them:

- **An image** is a snapshot of a filesystem plus a command to run. It is built from a Dockerfile,
  it is immutable, and it is made of layers so that a rebuild redoes only what changed.
- **A container** is a running (or stopped) copy of an image. It is cheap and disposable. Anything
  written inside a container that is not on a volume dies with it.
- **A volume** is where state lives on purpose: the database's files. `parking/` has one, named
  `pgdata`. It survives `down`; it does not survive `down -v`.
- **A compose file** describes several containers, their volumes, ports, environment, and the
  network in which they can find each other by service name. `app` reaches the database at `db:5432`
  because compose made `db` a hostname.

### 14.2 Once per machine

- **Mac and Windows:** Docker Desktop. On Windows it runs on the WSL 2 backend; turn that on in
  Desktop's settings, and run compose from the WSL side, in a project under the WSL home (`SHELL.md`
  — `/mnt/c` is slow, and for Docker's bind mounts it is very slow).
- **Linux:** Docker Engine plus the compose plugin, from Docker's repository, not the distribution's
  older package. Add yourself to the `docker` group so `sudo` is not needed.
- **Check:** `docker run --rm hello-world`, then `docker compose version`. Note the word: it is
  `docker compose` with a space; the hyphenated `docker-compose` is the old separate tool.
- **Know your architecture.** `docker version --format '{{.Server.Arch}}'` prints `arm64` on an
  Apple-silicon Mac and `amd64` on most everything else. Remember which you saw.

### 14.3 Once per repository

**A Dockerfile per service.** `parking/app/Dockerfile`, annotated:

```dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine            # the runtime, pinned to a major: same policy as PACKAGES.md
WORKDIR /srv/app               # every later path is relative to here
COPY app/package.json ./       # dependencies first, so this layer is cached until they change
RUN npm install --omit=dev     # (should be: COPY the lock file too, and `npm ci` — see PACKAGES.md)
COPY app/ ./                   # then the code, which changes often
ENV NODE_ENV=production
EXPOSE 3000                    # documentation; compose does the actual port mapping
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

The order matters. Docker caches each layer and reuses it when its inputs are unchanged, so copying
`package.json` and installing *before* copying the source means an edit to `index.js` does not
reinstall every dependency.

**The build context.** `parking/docker-compose.yml` sets `context: .` and `dockerfile:
app/Dockerfile`, so the context is `parking/`, not `parking/app/`. That is why the `COPY` paths
above start with `app/`. A Dockerfile cannot `COPY` from above its own context, and this layout lets
the image copy in the shared libraries (`contract/`, `identity/`) once the service depends on them.
Add a `.dockerignore` (`node_modules`, `.git`, `.env`) so the context sent to the builder is small
and never contains a secret.

**A compose file** naming the services, from `parking/docker-compose.yml`:

```yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: parking_user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: parking_pass                # the demo database; not a secret, and labeled
      POSTGRES_DB: parking
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data              # state, on a named volume
      - ./db/init.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init.sql:ro   # runs ONLY on an empty volume
    ports: ["5432:5432"]
  app:
    build: { context: ., dockerfile: app/Dockerfile }
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://parking_user:parking_pass@db:5432/parking
      JWT_SECRET: demo-secret-change-me              # a demo value, in plain text, on purpose
      PORT: 3000
    depends_on: [db]
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
volumes:
  pgdata:
```

`depends_on` orders *starting*, not *readiness*: `app` may come up before Postgres accepts
connections. The fix is a health check on `db` and `condition: service_healthy` on the dependency:

```yaml
  db:
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U parking_user -d parking"]
      interval: 2s
      retries: 15
  app:
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
```

That is the power-on self test from `TESTING.md`, applied to a dependency: do not start until the
thing you need says it is ready.

### 14.4 Every day

| Want                                 | Type                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| build and start everything           | `docker compose up --build`                                                                   |
| the same, in the background          | `docker compose up --build -d`, then `docker compose logs -f app`                             |
| stop, keep the data                  | `docker compose down`                                                                         |
| stop, **destroy the data**           | `docker compose down -v` — required after any schema change                                   |
| what is running                      | `docker compose ps`                                                                           |
| a shell in the database              | `docker compose exec db psql -U parking_user parking`                                         |
| a shell in the app                   | `docker compose exec app sh`                                                                  |
| rebuild from scratch                 | `docker compose build --no-cache`                                                             |
| edit the frontend without rebuilding | add a bind mount: `./app/public:/srv/app/public` under `app.volumes`, then reload the browser |
| reclaim disk                         | `docker system prune` (and `-a` to drop unused images too — it asks)                          |

**`down -v` is not a migration.** `db/init.sql` runs only when the volume is empty, so a schema
change with `up` and no `down -v` gives you new code against the old database, silently. `down -v`
fixes that by destroying the data, which is fine for a demo and not for anything with real rows.
`V-7` in `REQUIREMENTS.md` says the real story is still to be written.

#### Repeatable, almost

An image tag is a family, not a file. `node:20-alpine` on an Apple-silicon Mac pulls the `arm64`
build; on a GitHub runner it pulls `amd64`. Same Dockerfile, two architectures, two builds of every
package inside. They behave the same almost always; native modules, packages with no `arm64` build,
numerical libraries, and anything timing-sensitive are where they differ. Three honest choices:

| Choice                                                                                                        | Cost                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `platform: linux/amd64` on the service                                                                        | emulation on Apple silicon: slow, and now the developer's machine is the odd one out |
| build both, test both — `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64`, and an `arm64` runner in CI | two builds; the honest one                                                           |
| accept *almost*, and write down where it is load-bearing                                                      | nothing today; a K4 with a known blast radius                                        |

Any of the three is fine. Not knowing which one you chose is not. And an image is only as repeatable
as its inputs: the base tag floats to the newest `20.x`, and `npm install` without a lock file
resolves fresh every build. `PACKAGES.md` is the fix, and `TESTING.md` is the argument.

### 14.5 Danger Will Robinson

- **`docker compose down -v`** on a database with real data. There is no undo. Back up first.
- **A secret in an image.** `ENV`, `ARG`, or a copied `.env` lands in a layer, and layers are
  forever; anyone who can pull the image can read it. Secrets enter at *run* time, through the
  environment (`1PASSWORD.md`).
- **`latest`.** An image tag with no version is a different image every week.
- **Running as root inside the container** for a service that does not need it. Add a `USER` line.
- **A project under `/mnt/c`** with a bind mount. Every file access crosses the boundary twice.

### 14.6 When it goes wrong

| Symptom                                           | Cause                                            | Do                                                               |
