| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `port is already allocated`                       | something else on 3000 or 5432                   | `lsof -i :3000`; stop it, or change the host side of the mapping |
| `app` exits with `ECONNREFUSED` to `db`           | Postgres was not ready                           | the health check above                                           |
| the schema change did not take                    | the volume still has the old database            | `docker compose down -v && docker compose up --build`            |
| `no space left on device`                         | old images and build cache                       | `docker system prune`                                            |
| it built on a teammate's machine and not on yours | different architecture, or a floating base image | compare `docker version` arch; pin; see *Repeatable, almost*     |
| the container cannot see a file you just edited   | it was copied at build time                      | rebuild, or bind-mount the directory while iterating             |
| everything is slow on Windows                     | project under `/mnt/c`                           | move it to the WSL home                                          |

### 14.7 Checklist

- [ ] `docker compose up --build` works from a clean clone, and `http://localhost:3000` answers.
- [ ] `docker compose down -v` then `up` returns the seed state, and you know why `-v` matters.
- [ ] The Dockerfile copies the manifest and lock before the source, and installs with `npm ci`.
- [ ] `.dockerignore` exists and excludes `node_modules`, `.git`, and `.env`.
- [ ] The base image is pinned to a major, and you can name the architecture it was built for.
- [ ] No secret is in any image layer or compose file except the demo value, and the demo value is
      labeled as one.

### 14.8 In `parking/`

`T-5` — one command returns the entire system to a known state — is `docker compose down -v` and `up
--build`, which is why the essays keep calling the reset cheap. The compose file lists only the
services that exist and says which ones will join it, so `up` works from a clean checkout today.
`E-8` puts a one-hour window on anything that cannot be done live, and a schema change under real
data is the first thing that will not fit in `down -v`. And the `JWT_SECRET` line in the compose
file is the demo secret in plain text, labeled, which is the honest way to have one.

### 14.9 Resources

- Docker's *Dockerfile reference* and *Compose file reference* — every key above, defined.
- Docker's *Multi-platform images* page — the `arm64` and `amd64` story, from the source.
- The languages course repository's `rust/` directory — a container used for exactly what containers
  are best at, a hermetic build, with the reasoning written down; and its `ml/` directory, for when
  a container is the wrong tool.

## 15. Packages

Every project stands on code you did not write, and that code changes under you. A package manager
is how you say what you are compatible with, record what you actually installed, and take a fix when
one arrives — three different jobs, and the mistakes come from giving all three to one file.

- **The fear it retires:** "A different install broke it." And: "That CVE has been open for a year."
- **The fence you prove:** A lock file committed, an install that refuses when the lock and the
  manifest disagree, and one dependency update taken as a pull request with green tests.
- **Before this:** `DOCKER.md`
- **After this:** `AGENT.md`

### 15.1 The model

```
  manifest  ──resolver──▶  lock  ──install──▶  node_modules/ (or .pixi/, or target/)
  what you are              what you ran:       what is on this machine right now
  compatible with:          exact versions,
  ranges, by major.minor    with hashes,
                            per platform
  committed                 committed           ignored
```

Semantic versioning is the interface between you and strangers: `major.minor.revision`, where the
major changes when something breaks, the minor when something is added, and the revision when
something is fixed. So the policy, from `TESTING.md`:

> In the manifest, say what you are compatible with — the major, and the minor you need as a floor.
> In the lock, record what you ran — the revision, and the hash. Commit both.

| Policy in the manifest                                | Repeatable?      | When a CVE lands                                                   | In practice                   |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------- |
| nothing pinned: `*`, `latest`                         | no               | you already have the fix, and every breaking change                | red on Wednesday, no commit   |
| the revision pinned: `4.19.2`                         | yes, by hand     | someone edits every pin, everywhere, after reading every changelog | never                         |
| **major.minor in the manifest, revision in the lock** | yes, by the lock | `npm update`, run the suite, commit the lock: an hour              | a reviewable, revertible diff |

Repeatability against survivability. The middle row survives; the last row is the one that is both.

### 15.2 Once per machine

**Node.** Install a version manager rather than a bare Node, so the version is per project: `fnm` or
`nvm`. Then `fnm install 20` (or `nvm install 20`). `node --version` should print a `20.x`. The
major is the pin; the revision floats.

**pixi** (or conda) for anything Python, R, or with a compiled dependency that varies by hardware:
one installer from `pixi.sh`, then `pixi --version`. **cargo** comes with Rust via `rustup`. You
will not need all three today; you will need the habit that is the same in all three.

### 15.3 Once per repository

#### npm

`package.json` is the manifest. Ranges:

| Written       | Means              | Use                                           |
| ------------- | ------------------ | --------------------------------------------- |
| `^4.19.2`     | `>=4.19.2 <5.0.0`  | the default, and the policy: within the major |
| `~4.19.2`     | `>=4.19.2 <4.20.0` | within the minor; rarely needed               |
| `4.19.2`      | exactly this       | almost never; that is the lock file's job     |
| `*`, `latest` | anything           | never                                         |

`package-lock.json` is the lock. It is generated, it is committed, and it is never edited by hand.
Two commands, and the difference between them is the whole point:

| Command       | Does                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `npm install` | resolves from the manifest, **updates the lock**, installs. For adding or changing a dependency.                                                       |
| `npm ci`      | installs **exactly** the lock, and **refuses** if the lock and manifest disagree. For everyone else, every time, and in every Dockerfile and workflow. |

Pin the runtime too: an `engines` field in `package.json` (`"node": ">=20 <21"`) and a `.nvmrc` or
`.node-version` file containing `20`, so a teammate's version manager picks the same major.

**In `parking/app/`, at this writing, the lock file does not exist**, and `app/Dockerfile` runs `npm
install` from the manifest alone. Every image build resolves `express`, `jsonwebtoken`, and `pg`
fresh, and nothing records what it chose. The fix is three lines:

```sh
cd parking/app
npm install --package-lock-only        # write package-lock.json without touching node_modules
git add package-lock.json
```

then in `app/Dockerfile`, copy the lock beside the manifest and install with `npm ci`:

```dockerfile
COPY app/package.json app/package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
```

`parking/package.json`, the workspace root, has **no dependencies at all**, on purpose: the tests
use Node's built-in runner, so nothing has to be installed to run them. That is not minimalism; it
is one fewer thing to learn, trust, audit, and update, forever.

#### pixi

`pixi.toml` is the manifest; `pixi.lock` is the lock, with **one resolution per platform**. The same
policy, in its syntax:

```toml
[workspace]
platforms = ["osx-arm64", "linux-64", "win-64"]     # everything the lock will hold an answer for

[dependencies]
python = ">=3.12,<3.14"                             # major.minor floor, major ceiling
numpy  = ">=2,<3"
```

| Command                 | Does                                                             |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `pixi add numpy`        | edits the manifest and re-locks                                  |
| `pixi install --locked` | installs exactly the lock, refuses if it is stale — the `npm ci` |
| `pixi update`           | re-resolves within the ranges and rewrites the lock — the update |
| `pixi run test`         | runs a task from the manifest, in the environment                |

Reach for pixi instead of a container when a dependency differs by hardware, the toolchain is too
big for an image, the tool has a real window, or it needs a device the container cannot see. The
languages course repository's `ml/` directory is the worked example and says when *not* to.

#### cargo

`Cargo.toml` and `Cargo.lock`; `cargo build --locked` is the `npm ci`. Same shape.

### 15.4 Every day

- **Add a dependency as a proposal, not a decision.** `AGENTS.md`: each one is something a student
  must learn, trust, and audit. Prefer what is already there and the standard library. Look at the
  package's install scripts, its dependency count, and when it was last released before adding it.

- **Take updates on a schedule.** Weekly, by a named person or a bot. `.github/dependabot.yml` opens
  the pull request for you:

  ```yaml
  version: 2
  updates:
    - package-ecosystem: npm
      directory: /parking/app
      schedule:
        interval: weekly
  ```

  The suite runs on the pull request (`GITHUB-ACTIONS.md`); if it is green, merge it that day. That
  is the hour. A lock file that is never regenerated is a revision pin with extra steps.

- **`npm outdated`** shows what the ranges would allow; **`npm audit`** lists known vulnerabilities
  in the lock. Read the second one for severity and reachability, not for its count.

- **Never edit the lock by hand.** If a merge conflicts in it, take either side and regenerate: `npm
  install` (or `pixi lock`), then commit.

### 15.5 Danger Will Robinson

- **`npm install` in CI or in a Dockerfile.** It may rewrite the lock or ignore it. `npm ci`.
- **A lock file not committed.** Then there is no record of what you ran, and the container is
  repeatable only at the level of the operating system (`DOCKER.md`).
- **`rm -rf node_modules && npm install` as a fix.** It works because the lock drifted or the
  manifest changed; find out which, or it will happen to the next person.
- **A dependency added by an agent.** It is fluent about packages you have never heard of. Treat the
  addition as the proposal it is (`AGENT.md`).
- **Typosquats and install scripts.** A package one letter off from the one you meant, with a
  `postinstall` that runs on your machine. Read the name twice; check the weekly downloads.

### 15.6 When it goes wrong

| Symptom                                 | Cause                                                          | Do                                                                     |
| --------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `npm ci` fails: "lock file out of sync" | someone changed the manifest without re-locking                | `npm install`, commit the lock, then `npm ci` again                    |
| works after deleting `node_modules`     | lock drift, or a stale install                                 | use `npm ci`; find what changed                                        |
| `ERESOLVE` peer dependency conflict     | two packages want incompatible majors of a third               | read which; pick versions that agree; do not `--force`                 |
| a native module fails on `arm64`        | no prebuilt binary for the platform                            | `DOCKER.md`'s three choices; or a pure-JavaScript alternative          |
| green Tuesday, red Wednesday, no commit | something floated — a floating range with no lock, or `latest` | pin the major; commit the lock                                         |
| `npm audit` shows a hundred findings    | most are in dev tools and unreachable                          | fix the ones in runtime dependencies first; do not `audit fix --force` |

### 15.7 Checklist

- [ ] The manifest uses `^major.minor` ranges and no exact revisions.
- [ ] The lock file exists and is committed; the install in CI and in the Dockerfile is `npm ci`.
- [ ] The runtime major is pinned in `engines` and in a version file.
- [ ] Updates are scheduled — a bot or a named person — and the suite runs on each.
- [ ] You have merged one dependency update as a pull request, green, and could revert it in one
      commit.
- [ ] You can explain to a classmate why a pinned revision is the "never" row.

### 15.8 In `parking/`

Two manifests, two deliberate states. `parking/package.json` has zero dependencies so that the tests
run with nothing installed. `parking/app/package.json` has three, with `^` ranges — the right policy
— and no lock, which is the open finding `TESTING.md` names and this document fixes. The image's
base tag, `node:20-alpine`, is the same policy applied to the runtime: major pinned, revision
floats, `docker compose pull` is the update.

### 15.9 Resources

- semver.org — the eleven rules, and why a revision may float.
- npm's documentation on `package-lock.json` and `npm ci` — short, and the distinction is the whole
  subject.
- pixi's documentation on the lock file and multi-platform solves; the languages course repository's
  `ml/README.md` as the worked example.

## 16. Agents

An agent is an extremely fast writer with no stake in the outcome. It can read the repository, edit
files, run commands, and draft a change in less time than it takes you to read one. Everything in
this sequence so far — the shell, git, secrets, issues, checks, containers, packages — is what makes
that safe to use, and the failure mode of agents is skipping it.

- **The fear it retires:** "I could not have built this in the time I had." And the fear it
  *creates*, which this document is about: "working code nobody can explain."
- **The fence you prove:** An agent-drafted change, reviewed line by line, run, signed by you with
  the `Co-Authored-By` trailer, green in CI, merged through a pull request — and you can explain
  every line of it to a teammate.
- **Before this:** everything else in `essentials/`
- **After this:** `AGENTS.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md`, which are the working agreement this document
  sets up

### 16.1 The model

```
  you ──task, with a done sentence──▶ agent ──reads──▶ the repository: CLAUDE.md, the working set, code
   ▲                                    │
   │                                    ├──runs──▶ shell commands, tests, the container (if you allow)
   │                                    │
   └────── a diff, to review ◀──────────┘
   then: you read it, run it, sign it, own it.
```

Three facts decide how to work with one:

- **It arrives knowing nothing and leaves remembering nothing.** Every session starts from the
  repository. Anything not written there — a constraint in your head, a decision in chat — does not
  exist to it, and it will violate that constraint cleanly, with tests, before lunch.
- **It is a K3 factory.** Fluent, confident, plausible, and occasionally wrong is the precise shape
  of erroneous certainty, arriving faster than you can check it. "This should work" is not a run.
- **It is fastest at the bottom of the waterfall** — code, tests, fixtures, migrations, the second
  and third test case — and no help at all at the top, where the work is conversations with people
  and laws. It will normalize a schema in a minute and never ask about the registrar. The
  requirement document is the railing.

### 16.2 Once per machine

Install Claude Code, which is the agent this course uses; others follow the same shape.

```sh
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash          # mac, linux, WSL
```

```powershell
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex                  # windows powershell
```

`SHELL.md` told you to read a piped installer before running it. This is one; download it, read it,
then run it. Start the agent inside a repository by typing `claude` there. It works in the terminal
you already have, on the files git already tracks, and it asks before it edits a file or runs a
command. Those prompts are the default mode, and you should stay in it until the habits below are
habits.

### 16.3 Once per repository

1. **`CLAUDE.md`** is what the agent reads at the start of every session. `/init` drafts one by
   reading the codebase; this repository's says mechanics — how to run things, where things live,
   what the seams are — and its first line points at `AGENTS.md`, the working agreement. Claude Code
   reads `CLAUDE.md`; to make it read `AGENTS.md` mechanically rather than by instruction, put
   `@AGENTS.md` in `CLAUDE.md`.

2. **`AGENTS.md`** says who owns what: humans own the structure, agents author and advise, the
   smallest change that does the job, no speculative structure, dependencies as proposals, comment
   the why. It is the document you will most often quote back to the agent.

3. **The working set is in the repository.** `REQUIREMENTS`, `DESIGN`, `QUEUE`, `FINDINGS`. This is
   the agent's memory. A constraint that lives only in a head is a K2 to the agent.

4. **Permissions, written down.** `.claude/settings.json` in the project says what the agent may do
   without asking, and it is committed and reviewed like anything else:

   ```json
   { "permissions": { "allow": ["Bash(npm test)", "Bash(npm run check)"] } }
   ```

   Allow the things you would run yourself a hundred times a day. Do not allow `git push`.

5. **One command to run and one to reset** (`DOCKER.md`). An agent that cannot run the thing cannot
   check its own claim, and "never let confidence substitute for a run" needs a run to be possible.

### 16.4 Every day

The loop, and every step of it is one of the earlier essentials:

1. **Write the task as a done sentence, with the ID.** "`C-5`: values outside `[0, capacity]` are
   rejected and the lot marked degraded; a test named `C-5` fails without the change." Vague in,
   vague out. This is the acceptance criterion from `AGILE_VS_WATERFALL.md`, addressed to a machine.

2. **Ask for the smallest diff, one concern.** "Propose before restructuring." "Show me the test
   failing first." "Do not touch files I did not name." The agent will happily produce three hundred
   lines; a diff you cannot review is a diff you cannot sign (`GITHUB-ISSUES.md`).

3. **Read the whole diff.** Not the summary — the diff. If you cannot explain a line to a teammate,
   it does not go in. The line you skipped is the one that added a dependency, reformatted a file
   you did not ask about, or asserted nothing.

4. **Run it.** `npm run check`, the container, the fault you meant to inject. The agent's "this
   should work" is not a run; yours is.

5. **Ask the retro questions.** *What did you assume because nobody wrote it down? What did you have
   to read that you should not have needed?* Put the answers in the repository — `CLAUDE.md`, a
   README, `FINDINGS` — where the next session, human or not, will find them.

6. **Commit it yourself, with the trailer, and sign it.**

   ```
   C-5: reject out-of-range readings at the boundary

   Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
   ```

   The agent does not commit unless asked, and you should not ask. Your signature says *I have read
   this and I stand behind it*; the trailer says who drafted it. Both are true, and they are
   different claims.

7. **Open the pull request**, and let the reviewer ask the three questions. The reviewer treats an
   agent-drafted change exactly like any other, which is the point of having reviewed it yourself
   first.

#### What to hand it, and what not to

| Hand it                                                                                      | Keep                                                                    |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| the second and third test case, once you have written the first                              | the first one, which decides what the thing is                          |
| fixtures, seed data, fault scripts, the conformance harness                                  | the requirement the harness checks                                      |
| "which assumptions in `REQUIREMENTS.md` does this sentence invalidate?" — search-shaped work | the decision about what to do with the answer                           |
| a migration script, from a design you wrote down                                             | the schema design, and whether it is legal to keep the data             |
| translation packs, boilerplate, glue                                                         | the vocabulary — a new noun is a decision (`SOFTWARE-ENGINEERING-2.md`) |
| the retro questions                                                                          | the retro                                                               |

### 16.5 Danger Will Robinson

- **A secret in a prompt.** The prompt goes to a third party. Reference by name, never paste a value
  (`1PASSWORD.md`).
- **Skipping the prompts.** The mode that bypasses permission checks exists, and its flag is named
  `--dangerously-skip-permissions` for a reason: it lets the agent write to `.git`, to `.claude`,
  and to anything else without asking. It is for sandboxes you can throw away, not for the
  repository with your term's work in it.
- **Letting it push.** A push is a publication (`GIT.md`'s elephant). It is yours to do, after
  reading.
- **Signing what you have not read.** The signature is the whole mechanism of ownership in this
  repository. An unread diff under a good signature is worse than an unsigned one, because it spends
  the trust.
- **A test that names the ID and asserts nothing.** `T-3` can be gamed by a machine faster than by a
  person. Watch it fail first.
- **The five-minute flag.** Asked for a feature that touches a scope decision, an agent will add a
  boolean column and a table and be done before you have opened the requirements. That is the pivot
  in `docs/TEAM-AND-CLIENT.md` at machine speed; the costing table comes before the prompt.

### 16.6 When it goes wrong

| Symptom                                                  | Cause                                | Do                                                                                                  |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| it asserts something false about the code                | it did not open the file             | "never assert something about this code you have not opened" — `AGENTS.md`; ask it to show the line |
| the diff touches ten files you did not name              | scope creep, or reformatting         | reject; ask again with "only these files"                                                           |
| it added a dependency                                    | fluency                              | treat as a proposal; usually decline (`PACKAGES.md`)                                                |
| it "fixed" a failing test by weakening the assertion     | Goodhart on green                    | restore the assertion; the test was right                                                           |
| it changed a requirement to match the code               | the costume rule (`CONTRIBUTING.md`) | revert; if the requirement is wrong, that is a conversation with the client                         |
| the next session does not know what the last one decided | nothing was written down             | the working set; `FINDINGS`; a line in `CLAUDE.md`                                                  |
| it designed a schema before there was a requirement      | the waterfall, at machine speed      | stop; the railing (`AGILE_VS_WATERFALL.md`)                                                         |

### 16.7 Checklist

- [ ] `claude` starts in the repository, in the default permission mode.
- [ ] `CLAUDE.md` exists, points at `AGENTS.md`, and says how to run and reset the system.
- [ ] `.claude/settings.json` allows the test and check commands and nothing that publishes.
- [ ] You have written a task as a done sentence with a requirement ID and received a diff you could
      read in one sitting.
- [ ] You ran the result yourself before committing it.
- [ ] The commit carries the `Co-Authored-By` trailer and your signature, and the pull request
      passed review.
- [ ] You asked the two retro questions and put the answers in the repository.

### 16.8 In `parking/`

`AGENTS.md` is the working agreement and `CONTRIBUTING.md`'s *Working with agents* section is the
procedure: read the whole diff, credit the agent and keep the authority, ask for smaller drafts,
push back in the conversation and not in the commit. The essays give the reasons:
`SOFTWARE-ENGINEERING.md` on why an agent is a K3 factory and where to spend the time it saves, and
`AGILE_VS_WATERFALL.md` on why its arrival moves the human up the waterfall. And the repository's
own history is the demonstration: most of its documents were drafted with an agent, every one was
read and signed by a person, and the difference between those two facts is the subject of the whole
course.

### 16.9 Resources

- Claude Code's documentation — *Getting started*, *Settings*, and *Permissions* are the three pages
  the setup above is built on; they move faster than this document, so trust them where they
  disagree.
- `AGENTS.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md` in this repository.
- The *Working with agents* section of `SOFTWARE-ENGINEERING.md`, and *Ask your agents*, which is
  where the retro questions come from.

## Appendix A — Glossary

Terms the three parts define in passing, collected. Each is one line here and argued at length where
it first appears.

| Term                      | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **K0 … K4**               | The five kinds of not-knowing: the known; the known unknown; the unknown unknown; erroneous certainty; a falsehood kept on purpose. K0–K3 are in order of expense. K4 is a choice.      |
| **Observable behavior**   | Something you could check from outside without reading the source. Requirements are written in it; "the code is clean" is not.                                                          |
| **Contract**              | The promises one part of a system makes to another, written down: what it accepts, what it returns, and how it fails. Not the code that keeps them.                                     |
| **Working set**           | `REQUIREMENTS_vX`, `DESIGN_vX`, `QUEUE`, `FINDINGS` — the four documents that make a project's state observable from where every party stands, versioned with the code.                 |
| **Fence**                 | A checkpoint that proves something: a demo to a real client, a conformance run that exits nonzero, a deploy that happened. A status meeting is not one.                                 |
| **Iteration**             | A fixed period, one to two weeks, that ends at a fence: a running thing shown to the client, a diff to the requirements, a `FINDINGS` entry, a priced queue.                            |
| **Client**                | The person who can say yes, no, and how much. Their pain is evidence; their proposed solution is a guess.                                                                               |
| **Proportion mismatch**   | The client sizes a requirement by their world — spaces, dollars, minutes. The design sizes it by the assumptions it invalidates. The gap between the two is where K2 lives.             |
| **Read your K4s**         | Reading every scope decision and assumed falsehood back to the client as a question. Converts a K4 to a K1 at the price of one sentence.                                                |
| **Essential complexity**  | Difficulty that belongs to the problem and survives every rewrite. Test: name the requirement that would have to disappear for it to go away.                                           |
| **Accidental complexity** | Difficulty you introduced. Invisible to you because you understand it; charged to strangers, and to you in a month.                                                                     |
| **Conceptual integrity**  | One coherent design over every good idea. It shows up first in vocabulary — one thing, one word; one word, one thing — and somebody has to hold it.                                     |
| **Locality of reasoning** | Being able to be sure of a part without reading the whole. The real reason interfaces exist; reuse is a bonus.                                                                          |
| **Carry**                 | Everything a piece of software costs for as long as it exists: attention, review, upgrades, security surface, the chance it breaks a neighbor. Cost is build plus carry times lifetime. |
| **Cache**                 | Any copy of state that might not match the original. Naming one inherits its questions: how stale, how would you know, and what happens to the user meanwhile.                          |
| **Idempotent**            | Doing it twice equals doing it once, so "did that go through?" stops being a question. "Set available to 37" is; "one car arrived" is not.                                              |
| **One-way door**          | A decision that cannot be cheaply undone: a schema with data under it, a published interface, a distributed key, a released image. Deliberate in proportion to it.                      |
| **Provenance**            | Who said this, and can I check it later without asking them again — for a reading, a log record, a firmware image, and a commit alike.                                                  |
| **Designated liar**       | A component built to fail or lie on request so the handling of it can be seen to work. In `parking/`, the sensor; after the pivot, the gate as well.                                    |
| **Operating envelope**    | The client's numbers — how many, how badly it may break, how long it may be down — inside which every other requirement is read. Section `E` of the requirements.                       |
| **Availability budget**   | Tolerable downtime as a number with a period and a beneficiary. Unstated, it defaults to 100%, the most expensive requirement you can accidentally accept.                              |
| **Thin vertical slice**   | The bridge: click to route to SQL to response, built end to end first and then thickened. Horizontal layers all finish at the same time — never.                                        |
| **Mock**                  | A stand-in that answers, and misbehaves on request. A K4 by construction: a scheduling risk converted into an integration risk, a good trade only if you integrate continuously.        |
| **Flat schedule**         | Everything startable at once, because every dependency between components has been written down as an interface, a mock, or a failing test rather than sequenced.                       |
